1.module: Module 1: Getting Started with Kali Linux
1.about: The opening chapter answers the question every beginner asks: why Kali Linux? It explains what Kali is, where it came from, how it differs from Ubuntu, and which built-in security tools make it the standard operating system for penetration testing. It also sets expectations by naming who should use Kali and who should learn Linux fundamentals first.
learn: What Kali Linux is and how it relates to BackTrack Linux and Debian
Why security professionals choose Kali over a general-purpose distribution
How Kali Linux differs from Ubuntu in purpose and default tooling
The built-in tools used for penetration testing, forensics and security research
Who should use Kali and who should wait until they have Linux basics
Real-world use cases: penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, digital forensics and security research

concepts.h: Kali Linux is a tool collection, not a magic button
concepts.p: Kali Linux is a free, open-source, Debian-based distribution maintained by OffSec (formerly Offensive Security). Its value is that hundreds of security tools are pre-installed and pre-configured, which removes hours of setup work. The tools still require a human who understands networking, Linux and testing methodology, so Kali accelerates skilled work rather than replacing it.

Ubuntu is tuned for everyday desktop use and servers. Kali is tuned for security assessment: it ships with Nmap, Metasploit, Wireshark, Burp Suite and many other tools, and it is not intended as a daily-driver operating system. Both are Linux distributions, so learning one builds transferable skills for the other.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and does not require commands. It is the orientation lesson before you download anything.
practical.safety: Kali Linux is legal to download and use. Using its tools against systems you do not own or have written permission to test is illegal in many jurisdictions.

faq.q: Should a complete beginner start with Kali Linux?
faq.a: Kali is an excellent place to learn cybersecurity, but it is easier once you are comfortable with basic Linux concepts. This course starts from fundamentals, so a motivated beginner can follow along.

faq.q: Is Kali Linux only for hacking?
faq.a: No. It is used for authorized penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, digital forensics, incident response, security research and general Linux learning.

2.module: Module 1: Getting Started with Kali Linux
2.about: Chapter 2 clears up one of the most common beginner confusions: Linux is not Unix, but it is Unix-like. The lesson walks through the history of Unix at Bell Labs, the creation of the Linux kernel in 1991, the licensing and technical differences between the two, and where distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Kali fit in.
learn: What Unix is and how it started at Bell Labs in 1969
What Linux is and how it relates to the Unix design philosophy
The key technical and licensing differences between Unix and Linux
How Debian, Ubuntu and Kali Linux fit into the Linux distribution family
Why Unix-like systems dominate servers, cloud infrastructure and security work
Common myths and misconceptions about Unix and Linux

concepts.p: Linux was written from scratch by Linus Torvalds and does not contain the original Unix source code. It follows Unix design ideas — everything is a file, small tools combine through pipes, and a powerful shell drives the system — which is why it is described as Unix-like. The UNIX trademark itself is a certification managed by The Open Group.

concepts.h: Why the distinction matters for security work
concepts.p: Most servers, network appliances and cloud systems you assess run Linux or another Unix-like operating system. Understanding the shared philosophy makes file permissions, processes, logs and the command line easier to learn, and those are the foundations of every later chapter.

practical.intro: This is a history and terminology lesson. It does not introduce new commands, but it explains the system you will use for the rest of the course.
practical.safety: No offensive techniques are introduced in this chapter.

faq.q: Is Linux a copy of Unix?
faq.a: No. Linux is an independent kernel inspired by Unix design and combined with GNU userland tools. It shares concepts and interfaces but not the original Unix source code.

faq.q: Is macOS Unix?
faq.a: Yes. macOS is a certified Unix system. Linux is Unix-like but is not certified as UNIX.

2.seo_description: Unix vs Linux explained for beginners: history, licensing, technical differences, and where Kali Linux fits. Chapter 2 of the EINITIAL24 Kali course.

3.module: Module 1: Getting Started with Kali Linux
3.about: Downloading the wrong ISO is a real risk: fake Kali images can contain malware before you run your first command. Chapter 3 shows the official Kali download page, explains Installer, Live, Network Installer and pre-built Virtual Machine images, and demonstrates verifying the SHA256 checksum of a download.
learn: Why unofficial Kali downloads are dangerous
The official Kali Linux download page and how to recognise it
The difference between Installer, Live, Network Installer and Virtual Machine images
How to choose an image for a virtual machine versus bare-metal hardware
How to verify a download with its SHA256 checksum
Common beginner mistakes with mirrors, versions and file types

concepts.h: Choose the image that matches your plan
concepts.p: The Installer image installs Kali onto a disk. The Live image runs from removable media and can optionally install. The Network Installer downloads packages during installation and is small. Pre-built Virtual Machine images are ready to import into VirtualBox or VMware and are the quickest safe starting point for a lab.

Kali publishes a SHA256SUMS file next to its images. Computing the hash of your downloaded ISO and comparing it with the published value confirms the file arrived intact and matches what the Kali project signed. A mismatch means you should delete the file and download it again.

practical.intro: Download only from kali.org, then verify the image before importing or installing it.

commands.d: Print the SHA256 hash of the downloaded image.
Show the published hashes so you can compare them with your result.

practical.safety: Never disable your browser's download warnings to run an ISO from a third-party site. Verify the hash before you boot or import the image.

faq.q: Which Kali Linux image should a beginner download?
faq.a: For a first lab, the pre-built Virtual Machine image for VirtualBox or VMware is the simplest. Choose the Installer image if you plan to install Kali on real hardware.

faq.q: What if the checksum does not match?
faq.a: Do not use the file. Delete it, download again from the official site, and verify once more. A repeated mismatch suggests a corrupted download or a tampered source.

3.seo_title: How to Download Kali Linux Safely and Verify the ISO
3.seo_description: Download Kali Linux safely from the official site, choose the right image type, and verify the SHA256 checksum. Chapter 3 of the free Kali Linux tutorial series.

4.module: Module 1: Getting Started with Kali Linux
4.about: A virtual machine lets you practise offensive security without risking your main computer. Chapter 4 installs VirtualBox on Windows, macOS and Linux, adds the Extension Pack, and walks through the settings that matter: memory, processor cores, display, and the difference between NAT, Bridged and Host-Only networking.
learn: Why a virtual machine is the right place to run Kali Linux as a beginner
How to download and install VirtualBox from the official site
How to install the VirtualBox Extension Pack
Which memory, CPU and display settings to check before starting a VM
NAT, Bridged and Host-Only network modes and when to use each
Common installation errors and how to fix them

concepts.p: NAT gives the guest internet access through the host and hides it behind the host's address, which is convenient but limits inbound connections. Bridged mode puts the guest directly on your physical network, which is useful for network labs but exposes it to that network. Host-Only creates a private network between host and guest and is ideal for isolated practice.

Give Kali enough RAM (typically 2–4 GB) and at least two CPU cores if your host allows it. Enable 3D acceleration only if your GPU and drivers support it. Snapshots let you roll back after experiments, so take one immediately after installation.

practical.intro: The chapter is a guided installation. Keep VirtualBox and the Extension Pack at matching versions to avoid driver and USB problems.
practical.safety: Keep your lab VM on a Host-Only or NAT network until you understand the network modes. Never bridge a testing VM onto a network you do not own.

faq.q: Do I need VirtualBox to learn Kali Linux?
faq.a: No, but it is the most common free option. VMware and Hyper-V also work, and Kali can run on bare metal if you accept the risk.

faq.q: Which network mode should I use for a hacking lab?
faq.a: Host-Only for isolated practice, NAT for internet access without exposing the VM. Bridged only on networks you control and are authorized to test.

4.seo_title: Install VirtualBox for Kali Linux: Settings and Network Modes
4.seo_description: Set up VirtualBox for Kali Linux: installation on Windows, macOS and Linux, Extension Pack, RAM and CPU settings, plus NAT vs Bridged vs Host-Only networking.

5.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
5.about: Chapter 5 removes the fear of the terminal. It separates three terms beginners often mix up — terminal, shell and command line — shows how to open and navigate a terminal in Kali Linux, explains how to read the prompt, and introduces shortcuts that make command-line work faster.
learn: Why ethical hackers work from the terminal
The difference between terminal, shell and command line
How to open and navigate a terminal in Kali Linux
How to read a shell prompt and understand your current location
Keyboard shortcuts that speed up command entry
How to practise safely in a virtual machine without fear of breaking your host

concepts.p: The terminal is the window that accepts text and displays output. The shell is the program inside it that interprets commands, such as Bash or Zsh. The command line is the interface itself — the line where you type. Understanding the separation helps when you change shells or read documentation.

A typical Kali prompt shows the username, hostname and current directory, ending in $ for a normal user or # for root. If you see #, you are operating with full administrative power, so slow down and check each command before pressing Enter.

practical.intro: This chapter is about orientation and confidence. Open a terminal in your lab VM and practise reading the prompt.
practical.safety: Practice in a virtual machine and take a snapshot before experimenting. Destructive mistakes then cost you a rollback, not your data.

faq.q: Do I have to use the terminal in Kali Linux?
faq.a: You can use graphical tools, but most security tooling is designed for the command line. Terminal skills make you faster and more precise.

faq.q: What does the # symbol in the prompt mean?
faq.a: It usually means you are running as root, the administrative account. Commands run as root can change or break the system, so verify them first.

5.seo_title: Linux Terminal for Beginners: Terminal vs Shell vs CLI
5.seo_description: Learn the Linux terminal from scratch: terminal vs shell vs command line, reading the prompt, navigating Kali Linux, and beginner shortcuts that save time.

6.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
6.about: Every Kali tool is launched from a shell, so Chapter 6 builds the command vocabulary the rest of the course depends on. It groups 22 essential commands by task — navigation, file creation and deletion, copying and viewing, searching, permissions, and system information — with examples you can run in your own VM.
learn: Navigate the file system with pwd, ls and cd
Create and remove directories and files with mkdir, rmdir, touch and rm
Copy, move and read files with cp, mv, cat and nano
Search file contents and the file system with grep and find
Read text with less and more
Understand permissions with chmod and chown
Inspect the system with whoami, uname, uptime, df and du

concepts.p: Linux tools do one job and communicate through text. ls lists, grep filters, sort orders and less pages. Pipes let you chain them, which is why a handful of commands can answer complex questions without a dedicated tool.

concepts.h: Permissions are part of daily work
concepts.p: Every file has an owner, a group and a permission set for user, group and others. chmod changes permissions and chown changes ownership. Security work constantly touches these settings, from making a script executable to understanding why a service cannot read a file.

practical.intro: Run these in a scratch directory inside your Kali VM. They are the highest-value commands to memorise first.

commands.d: Print the current working directory.
List all files, including hidden ones, in long format.
Change into the /tmp directory.
Create a directory and move into it.
Create an empty file.
Copy a file.
Search a file for text, ignoring case.
Show the current user.
Show disk usage in human-readable units.

practical.safety: rm permanently deletes files; Linux has no recycle bin by default. Check your path with pwd before deleting anything.

faq.q: How many Linux commands do I need for Kali Linux?
faq.a: A few dozen cover most beginner work. Start with navigation, file handling, permissions and text search, then add tools as the course introduces them.

faq.q: What is the difference between cp and mv?
faq.a: cp creates a copy and leaves the original in place. mv moves the file or renames it, so the original path no longer exists.

7.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
7.about: Chapter 7 takes the most-used Linux command and explains it properly. You see the basic listing, then the meaning of ls -l, ls -a, ls -la and ls -lh, followed by the everyday companions cd, pwd, clear and history. The lesson finishes with common beginner mistakes and how to avoid them.
learn: What ls does and when to use each common flag
How to read the long listing produced by ls -l
How hidden files work and why ls -a shows them
The practical difference between ls -la and ls -lh
How cd, pwd, clear and history fit into a daily workflow
How to combine flags and avoid common mistakes

concepts.p: The long format shows permissions, link count, owner, group, size, modification time and name. The first character tells you whether the entry is a directory, a regular file or a link. This output is the starting point for almost every permission problem you will debug.

On Linux, a leading dot in a filename hides it from a plain ls. Configuration files such as .bashrc are hidden by convention, not by a special attribute. ls -a reveals them, and ls -la combines that with details.

practical.intro: Practise these in your home directory and watch how the output changes.

commands.d: List visible entries in the current directory.
Long listing with permissions, owner, size and date.
Include hidden dotfiles.
Long listing with human-readable sizes.
Confirm where you are before listing.
Show recently used commands.

practical.safety: Listing files is read-only and safe. Be careful when combining flags with commands that modify files.

faq.q: What does ls -lh do differently from ls -l?
faq.a: It prints file sizes in human-readable units such as KB, MB and GB instead of raw bytes.

faq.q: Why can't I see my configuration files?
faq.a: They start with a dot and are hidden from plain ls output. Use ls -a or ls -la to display them.

7.seo_description: Master the Linux ls command: long listings, hidden files, human-readable sizes and the everyday commands cd, pwd, clear and history. Kali Linux chapter 7.

8.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
8.about: Getting lost in the file system is the classic beginner problem, and cd is the fix. Chapter 8 explains absolute versus relative paths, the shortcuts cd .., cd ~ and cd -, and how to create files instantly with touch. A short recap of mkdir, rmdir and rm connects navigation to file management.
learn: How cd moves between directories
The difference between absolute and relative paths
The shortcuts cd .., cd ~ and cd -
How to create empty files with touch
How mkdir, rmdir and rm complement navigation
Common path mistakes and how to recover from them

concepts.p: An absolute path starts at the root, for example /etc/apt. A relative path begins from your current directory, for example ../logs. Absolute paths work from anywhere; relative paths are shorter but depend on where you are.

A single dot means the current directory, two dots mean the parent, tilde means your home directory and a dash returns to the previous directory. These are shell conveniences that keep long paths manageable.

practical.intro: Run these from your home directory and use pwd after each move to confirm your location.

commands.d: Show the current directory.
Move using an absolute path.
Move up one directory.
Return to your home directory.
Switch back to the previous directory.
Create an empty file in the current directory.

practical.safety: Navigation is safe. Deleting still uses rm, so check pwd before running destructive commands.

faq.q: What is the fastest way back to my home directory?
faq.a: Run cd with no arguments or use cd ~. Both return you to your home directory.

faq.q: What does cd - do?
faq.a: It switches to the directory you were in before the current one, which is useful when toggling between two working folders.

8.seo_title: Linux cd Command Explained: Absolute vs Relative Paths
8.seo_description: Learn the Linux cd command: absolute and relative paths, cd .., cd ~, cd - and touch, with practical examples for Kali Linux beginners.

9.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
9.about: Chapter 9 is a safety lesson disguised as a file-management lesson. It shows mkdir and rm, explains what the -r, -f and -rf options really do, demonstrates rm -i as a confirmation prompt, and warns about the classic mistake of deleting the wrong directory. clear closes the lesson.
learn: How to create single and nested directories with mkdir
How to delete files with rm and directories with rmdir
What rm -r, rm -f and rm -rf actually do
How rm -i adds a confirmation prompt before deletion
How to clean the terminal with clear
Which mistakes cause irreversible data loss

concepts.p: rm unlinks a file immediately. Unlike a desktop trash can, there is no restore step. That is why careful operators verify the path, use tab completion, and prefer rm -i when they are unsure.

The -r flag makes deletion recursive so it can remove directories and their contents. The -f flag suppresses prompts and ignores missing files. Combined as rm -rf, the command is fast, silent and unforgiving — never run it with a path you have not checked.

practical.intro: Create a disposable directory tree and practise deletion there only.

commands.d: Create nested directories in one command.
Create a test file.
Delete a single file.
Remove an empty directory.
Remove a directory tree with a prompt for each item.
Clear the terminal display.

practical.safety: rm -rf permanently destroys data. Never run it as root with a wildcard or an unchecked variable, and never on / or your home directory.

faq.q: Does rm move files to a trash folder?
faq.a: No. rm deletes the directory entry immediately. Recovering the data requires specialised tools and is not guaranteed.

faq.q: Why does rmdir fail?
faq.a: rmdir only removes empty directories. Use rm -r for a directory that still contains files.

9.seo_title: Linux rm Command: Delete Files Safely (rm -rf Explained)
9.seo_description: Understand Linux deletion: mkdir, rm, rmdir, rm -r, rm -f and rm -rf, plus the rm -i safety prompt. Learn why Linux has no recycle bin.

10.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
10.about: Chapter 10 covers copying and reading files. You see cp for single files, cp -r for directories, and cp -v for visible progress, then cat for short files and less, head and tail for longer ones. It also reinforces checking your location with pwd before running a command.
learn: How to copy files and directories with cp
What the -r and -v options do
How to view a whole short file with cat
How to page through long files with less
How to read the beginning and end of a file with head and tail
Why checking pwd first prevents copy mistakes

concepts.p: cp copies files by default. A directory contains other entries, so it must be copied recursively with -r. The -v flag prints each file as it is processed, which is useful when copying a large tree.

cat prints a file to the terminal and is ideal for short configuration snippets. less opens a pager with search and scrolling, while head and tail show only the start or end. Reading logs often starts with tail.

practical.intro: Create a small text file, then copy and read it in different ways.

commands.d: Confirm the working directory first.
Copy a file in the same directory.
Copy a directory recursively.
Copy with verbose output.
Print a short file.
Page through a long file. Press q to quit.
Show the first 20 lines.
Show the last 20 lines.

practical.safety: cp overwrites an existing destination without asking. Check the destination path before copying important files.

faq.q: Why does cp say 'omitting directory'?
faq.a: You tried to copy a directory without -r. Use cp -r to copy the directory and its contents.

faq.q: What is the difference between cat and less?
faq.a: cat prints the entire file at once. less lets you scroll and search without filling the terminal buffer.

10.seo_title: Linux cp Command: Copy Files and Folders (cp -r Explained)
10.seo_description: Learn how to copy files and folders in Linux with cp, cp -r and cp -v, then read them with cat, less, head and tail. Beginner-friendly Kali Linux guide.

11.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
11.about: Chapter 11 solves the lost-file problem. It shows locate for fast name searches, explains why updatedb keeps that database accurate, and introduces find for searches that need more control. The lesson closes with mv, including moving and renaming files and how mv differs from cp.
learn: How to find files by name with locate
Why the locate database can be stale and how updatedb fixes it
How find searches the live file system with more control
When to choose locate and when to choose find
How to move files and directories with mv
How to rename files and why mv differs from cp

concepts.p: locate queries a pre-built index, so it is extremely fast but only as current as the last updatedb run. find walks the actual file system, which is slower but always current and supports filters for size, type, permissions and modification time.

mv changes a file's path. If the destination is another directory, the file moves into it. If the destination is a new name in the same directory, the file is renamed. Unlike cp, no copy remains at the original path.

practical.intro: Practise searching for files you created, then move and rename them.

commands.d: Search the locate index for a filename.
Refresh the locate database after creating new files.
Search the current tree for text files.
Move a file into a directory.
Rename a file in place.

practical.safety: mv overwrites an existing destination silently. Use mv -i when moving important files between directories.

faq.q: Why does locate not find a file I just created?
faq.a: Its database has not been refreshed. Run sudo updatedb, or use find for an immediate live search.

faq.q: Can mv rename a directory?
faq.a: Yes. Moving a directory to a new name in the same parent directory renames it, including all its contents.

11.seo_title: Find Files in Linux Fast: locate, find and updatedb
11.seo_description: Learn how to find files in Linux with locate and find, refresh the database with updatedb, and move or rename files with mv. Kali Linux chapter 11.

12.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
12.about: Why does sort put 10 before 2? Chapter 12 answers that question and turns the confusion into a practical lesson on text processing. It covers alphabetical sorting, numeric sorting with -n, reverse order with -r, column selection with -k, duplicate removal with -u, and combining sort with other commands through pipes.
learn: Why default sort is lexicographic rather than numeric
How to sort text alphabetically with sort
How to sort numbers correctly with sort -n
How to reverse output with -r
How to sort by a specific column with -k
How to remove duplicate lines with -u and combine commands with pipes

concepts.p: By default sort compares text character by character, so "10" comes before "2" because "1" sorts before "2". The -n flag tells sort to interpret fields as numbers, which is what you want for sizes, counts and ports.

The pipe operator sends the output of one command into another. For example, a command that lists login attempts can be piped into sort and then into uniq to count repeated addresses. This composition is the heart of Unix-style text processing.

practical.intro: Create a small list of numbers and words, then compare the output of each option.

commands.d: Sort lines alphabetically.
Sort numerically.
Sort in reverse order.
Sort by the second column numerically.
Sort and remove duplicate lines.
Extract usernames and sort them using a pipe.

practical.safety: These commands only read input. Combine them with redirection carefully, because > overwrites the target file.

faq.q: Why does sort put 10 before 2?
faq.a: Default sort compares text, not numbers. Add -n to sort numerically.

faq.q: How do I remove duplicates while sorting?
faq.a: Use sort -u, or sort followed by uniq if you need to count occurrences.

12.seo_description: Fix the classic '10 before 2' problem and learn Linux sort: numeric sorting with -n, reverse with -r, columns with -k, duplicates with -u and pipes.

13.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
13.about: Chapter 13 handles archives entirely from the terminal. It shows how to zip single and multiple files, compress a whole directory with zip -r, inspect an archive with unzip -l, extract into a chosen directory with unzip -d, and install zip or unzip when they are missing.
learn: How to compress one or more files with zip
How to archive a directory recursively with zip -r
How to extract archives with unzip
How to list archive contents without extracting
How to extract to a specific directory with unzip -d
How to install zip and unzip if they are missing

concepts.p: A ZIP file bundles multiple files and compresses them. Extracting restores the directory structure stored inside the archive, which is why paths matter when you create it. Listing the archive first is a safe way to see what it contains before writing files to disk.
Archives from untrusted sources can contain unexpected paths. Listing contents with unzip -l and extracting into a dedicated directory reduces the risk of overwriting existing files.

practical.intro: Practise in a small directory so you can see exactly what each archive contains.

commands.d: Compress two files into one archive.
Compress a directory recursively.
List archive contents without extracting.
Extract into the current directory.
Extract into a specific directory.
Install the tools if they are missing.

practical.safety: Do not extract unknown archives into your home directory. List them first and use a disposable directory.

faq.q: What is the difference between zip and tar?
faq.a: zip both archives and compresses. tar traditionally archives only and is usually combined with gzip or xz for compression.

faq.q: Why does zip skip my folder?
faq.a: Without -r, zip does not descend into directories. Use zip -r to include the folder and its contents.

13.seo_title: How to Zip and Unzip Files in Linux (zip -r, unzip -d)
13.seo_description: Create and extract archives in Linux: zip, zip -r, unzip, unzip -l and unzip -d, plus installing zip and unzip on Kali Linux.

14.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
14.about: Linux remembers the commands you type, and Chapter 14 shows how to use that record. It covers viewing history, re-running commands with !! and history numbers, clearing the list with history -c, and finding where a program lives with whereis. It also compares whereis, which and locate.
learn: How to view your shell command history
How to re-run the last command or a specific numbered command
What history -c clears and what it does not
How whereis locates a program's binary, source and manual files
The difference between whereis, which and locate
When each of these commands is genuinely useful

concepts.p: The shell stores recent commands in memory and writes them to a history file. That is useful for repeating work, but it also means sensitive commands can persist in your account. Clearing history removes the list, not every trace written elsewhere by other tools or logging systems.

which reports the executable that your shell would run from PATH. whereis searches standard locations for binaries, source and manuals. locate searches a filesystem index. They answer different questions, so choosing the right one saves time.

practical.intro: Use history deliberately and avoid storing secrets in commands.

commands.d: Show recent commands with line numbers.
Re-run the previous command.
Re-run command number 42 from history.
Clear the in-memory history list.
Locate the binary and manual page for nmap.
Show which python3 your PATH resolves to.

practical.safety: Do not type passwords directly on the command line. They can be captured in shell history and process lists.

faq.q: Does history -c delete the history file?
faq.a: It clears the current session's list. The history file may still contain earlier commands until it is overwritten or removed.

faq.q: Why do whereis and which return different paths?
faq.a: which follows your PATH and reports what would execute. whereis searches a fixed set of standard directories for binaries, source and manuals.

14.seo_title: Linux history Command: Reuse, Clear and Find Programs
14.seo_description: Learn Linux command history: view past commands, reuse them with !! and !n, clear with history -c, and locate programs with whereis and which.

15.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
15.about: Chapter 15 introduces user accounts, the backbone of Linux access control. It demonstrates creating a user with adduser, contrasts adduser with the lower-level useradd, sets and changes passwords with passwd, switches users with su, and explains when to use su versus sudo. Root access and its risks close the lesson.
learn: How to create a user account with adduser
The difference between adduser and useradd
How to set and change passwords with passwd
How su works and how su - differs from su
When to use su and when to use sudo
Why root access requires care and least privilege

concepts.p: adduser is a friendly interactive wrapper that creates a home directory, sets a password and configures defaults. useradd is the low-level utility and does much less unless you pass explicit options. For normal administration, adduser is harder to get wrong.

su switches your identity to another account and asks for that account's password. sudo runs a single command with elevated privileges and asks for your own password, with the action logged. sudo with least privilege is usually safer and more auditable.

practical.intro: Run these inside your lab VM and inspect the resulting entries in /etc/passwd.

commands.d: Create a new user with a home directory and password prompt.
Set or change the user's password.
Start a login shell as student with their environment.
List the commands your account may run with sudo.
Show your user ID, group ID and group memberships.

practical.safety: Do not enable direct root login or share root passwords. Use sudo for individual commands and remove accounts you no longer need.

faq.q: What is the difference between su and su -?
faq.a: su keeps much of your current environment. su - starts a full login shell for the target user, including their home directory and environment variables.

faq.q: Should I work as root all the time?
faq.a: No. Use a normal account and sudo for specific tasks. Permanent root sessions make accidental damage and credential exposure far more likely.

15.seo_title: How to Create a User in Linux: adduser, passwd and su
15.seo_description: Create and manage Linux users: adduser vs useradd, passwd, su vs su -, and why sudo and least privilege matter. Chapter 15 of the Kali Linux course.

16.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
16.about: Chapter 16 explains the permission denied error from the ground up. It shows how to read the permission string in ls -l, what read, write and execute mean for files and directories, how numeric modes such as 755 and 644 are calculated, how symbolic modes work, how to make a script executable, and why chmod 777 is a bad habit. exit closes the session.
learn: How to read the ten-character permission string
What read, write and execute mean for files and directories
How octal permissions such as 755 and 644 are built
How numeric and symbolic chmod modes differ
How to make a script executable
Why chmod 777 is dangerous and how exit ends a session

concepts.p: Permissions are assigned to the owner (user), the group and others. Each gets read, write and execute bits. For a file, execute means it can run as a program. For a directory, execute means you can enter it and read means you can list its contents.

Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1. Add the values for each triad: 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x, 6 is rw- and 4 is r--. That is why 755 means owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x. 777 grants everyone full access and is almost never appropriate.

practical.intro: Practise on a disposable script and a test file. Check each change with ls -l.

commands.d: Inspect the current permissions.
Set owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x.
Set owner rw-, group r--, others r--.
Add execute permission for the relevant users.
Add execute only for the owner.

practical.safety: Avoid chmod 777. It lets any local user modify or execute the target and often hides a deeper ownership or design problem.

faq.q: What does chmod 755 mean?
faq.a: The owner can read, write and execute; group and other users can read and execute. It is common for scripts and directories that should be usable but not world-writable.

faq.q: Why is chmod 777 bad?
faq.a: It gives every user write and execute access. That enables tampering, privilege escalation and accidental damage.

16.seo_title: chmod Explained: Linux File Permissions 755, 644 and +x
16.seo_description: Understand Linux file permissions and chmod: read the ls -l string, calculate 755 and 644, use symbolic modes, make scripts executable and avoid chmod 777.

17.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
17.about: Chapter 17 goes deeper into symbolic permissions. Starting from a string like -rwxr-xr--, it explains the user, group and others triads, then shows how to add, remove and set permissions with +, - and =, including combined changes such as u+x,g-w. Before-and-after ls -l output makes the effect visible.
learn: How to read a permission string character by character
What u, g, o and a mean in symbolic mode
How to add permissions with +
How to remove permissions with -
How to set exact permissions with =
How to combine several changes in one chmod command

concepts.p: Symbolic changes modify the existing mode instead of replacing it. u+x adds execute for the owner and leaves every other bit untouched. That makes symbolic mode safer when you only need to adjust one permission.
The = operator sets a triad exactly. o=r removes write and execute from others and leaves read. Combining classes, such as ug=rw, applies the same exact setting to both.

practical.intro: Watch the permission string change after every command.

commands.d: Record the starting permissions.
Add execute for the owner only.
Remove write from the group.
Set others to read only.
Apply several changes in one command.
Add read for all classes.

practical.safety: Symbolic changes are precise but easy to mistype. Check the result with ls -l, especially on shared or system files.

faq.q: What does the a in chmod a+r mean?
faq.a: It means all three classes together: user, group and others.

faq.q: What is the difference between + and = in chmod?
faq.a: Plus adds a permission to what already exists. Equals sets the triad to exactly the permissions you list, removing anything else.

17.seo_title: chmod u+x, g-w, o=r: Symbolic Permissions Explained
17.seo_description: Read permission strings like -rwxr-xr-- and change them with chmod u+x, g-w, o=r, = and combined symbolic modes. Clear examples for Kali Linux beginners.

18.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
18.about: Chapter 18 turns permission theory into troubleshooting. Four worked examples show how to make a script executable, restrict a sensitive file, change an entire folder with chmod -R, and share a folder with a group. It then walks through diagnosing permission denied errors and verifying every change with ls -l.
learn: How to grant read, write and execute permissions on files
How to change permissions recursively with chmod -R
How to make a script executable and run it
How to restrict a sensitive file to its owner
How to share a folder with a group using ownership and permissions
How to diagnose the cause of a permission denied error

concepts.p: A directory's execute bit controls whether you can traverse it. If a parent directory lacks execute for your account, you cannot reach a file inside even when the file itself is readable. Permission problems often live one level above the file named in the error.

chmod -R applies the same mode to every item below a path. It is fast and blunt: executable bits may land on data files and sensitive subfolders may become readable. Apply it deliberately and verify with find or ls -l.

practical.intro: Use a disposable tree under your home directory to practise each scenario.

commands.d: Make a script executable by its owner.
Allow only the owner to read and write.
Apply a consistent mode to a folder tree.
Give a group ownership of a folder.
Inspect directory permissions and ownership.

practical.safety: chmod -R on system paths can break services. Restrict recursive changes to directories you created and understand.

faq.q: Why can I read a file but still get permission denied?
faq.a: One of the parent directories probably lacks execute permission for your account. Check the path one level at a time with ls -ld.

faq.q: How do I share a folder with only one group?
faq.a: Set group ownership with chgrp and use a mode such as 750 or 770 so group members get the access they need without exposing the folder to everyone.

18.seo_title: Fix Permission Denied in Linux: Practical chmod Examples
18.seo_description: Fix 'permission denied' in Linux with practical chmod examples: executable scripts, restricted files, recursive changes and group-shared folders.

19.module: Module 2: Linux Fundamentals for Ethical Hackers
19.about: Chapter 19 is a productivity chapter. It covers Tab completion, the arrow keys, Ctrl+R history search, Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E for line navigation, Ctrl+U and Ctrl+K for deleting text, Ctrl+L to clear the screen, Ctrl+C to stop a running command, and !! and !n to repeat commands.
learn: How to auto-complete commands and filenames with Tab
How to reuse earlier commands with the arrow keys
How to search command history with Ctrl+R
How to jump to the start or end of a line
How to delete text quickly with Ctrl+U and Ctrl+K
How to stop a stuck command with Ctrl+C

concepts.p: These key bindings come from the Readline library used by Bash and many other shells. They work in most Linux terminals, so the time invested pays off across distributions and tools.

Pressing Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground process. Most programs stop, but some ignore it or need a different signal. Knowing how to interrupt a runaway scan or a frozen pager is basic operational safety.

practical.intro: Practise each shortcut until it becomes muscle memory. No special setup is required.

commands.d: Search backwards through command history.
Jump to the beginning or end of the current line.
Delete text before or after the cursor.
Clear the screen without losing the current line.
Interrupt the running foreground command.

practical.safety: Ctrl+C interrupts, it does not undo. If a command has already changed files, restore from a snapshot or backup.

faq.q: What is the difference between Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z?
faq.a: Ctrl+C interrupts and usually terminates the process. Ctrl+Z suspends it and returns you to the shell, where it can be resumed with fg or bg.

faq.q: Does Tab completion work for command options?
faq.a: It completes commands and paths by default. Many shells can also complete options when completion packages are installed.

19.seo_title: Linux Terminal Shortcuts: Ctrl+R, Tab, Ctrl+C and More
19.seo_description: Speed up Linux terminal work with Tab completion, Ctrl+R history search, line editing shortcuts, Ctrl+C and command repetition. Beginner-friendly guide.

20.about: Chapter 20 opens the networking section with a question beginners often get wrong: does Kali Linux make you anonymous? It explains what anonymity actually means, how your IP address, DNS requests and browser fingerprint can expose you, and how anonymity differs from privacy and security. VPNs, proxies and Tor are introduced at a high level.
learn: What anonymity means in cybersecurity
Why security researchers and penetration testers care about it
How IP addresses, DNS requests and browser fingerprints reveal information
The difference between anonymity, privacy and security
How VPNs, proxies and Tor differ at a high level
The legal and ethical boundaries of anonymity tooling

concepts.h: Kali is not an anonymity system
concepts.p: Kali is a distribution full of security tools. It does not change how your traffic is routed. Unless you deliberately use Tor, a VPN or another proxy, your requests leave your network with your normal public IP address and your DNS queries follow your system configuration.

Security protects data from unauthorized access. Privacy controls who can collect and share information about you. Anonymity hides who you are. A VPN can improve privacy on a local network without making you anonymous to the VPN provider, which is why the three terms should not be used interchangeably.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual. It prepares you to evaluate the tools in chapters 21 to 29 instead of trusting labels.
practical.safety: Anonymity tools do not legalize activity. Laws apply regardless of how your traffic is routed, and no tool provides perfect anonymity.

faq.q: Does Kali Linux hide my IP address automatically?
faq.a: No. Kali does not route your traffic through Tor or a VPN unless you configure it to. Your public IP is visible to destinations by default.

faq.q: Is a VPN the same as anonymity?
faq.a: No. A VPN hides your IP from the destination but the provider can still see your traffic and identity. It is a privacy tool, not a guarantee of anonymity.

20.seo_title: Is Kali Linux Anonymous? Tor vs VPN vs Proxy Explained
20.seo_description: Does Kali Linux make you anonymous? Learn how IP addresses, DNS leaks and browser fingerprints expose you, and how Tor, VPNs and proxies differ.

21.about: Chapter 21 explains the proxy server: what it is, how requests flow through it, and why a website sees the proxy's address instead of yours. It covers HTTP, HTTPS and SOCKS proxies, the difference between forward and reverse proxies, common real-world uses, and the limits of using a proxy for anonymity.
learn: What a proxy is and how a request travels through it
How a proxy server changes the IP address a website sees
The difference between HTTP, HTTPS and SOCKS proxies
Forward proxy versus reverse proxy
Where proxies are used in real networks
What a proxy cannot protect you from

concepts.p: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and forwards their requests outward; it is what people usually mean by a proxy. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers, accepts requests on their behalf and is common for load balancing, caching and TLS termination.

concepts.h: A proxy is not anonymity by itself
concepts.p: The destination sees the proxy's address, but the proxy operator sees your address and traffic metadata. Logs, browser fingerprints and unencrypted content can still identify you. Chaining proxies adds complexity without guaranteeing privacy.

practical.intro: This is a conceptual chapter. It defines the terminology used by Proxychains later in the course.
practical.safety: Free public proxies are frequently operated by unknown parties and may inspect or modify traffic. Avoid sending credentials through them.

faq.q: Does a proxy hide my IP address from websites?
faq.a: It hides your address from the destination, which sees the proxy instead. The proxy itself still knows your address.

faq.q: What is the difference between HTTP and SOCKS proxies?
faq.a: HTTP proxies are designed for web traffic and understand HTTP semantics. SOCKS proxies forward arbitrary TCP connections, so they can carry more protocols.

21.seo_title: Proxy Server Explained: How It Hides Your IP (and Limits)
21.seo_description: What is a proxy server and how does it hide your IP? Compare HTTP, HTTPS and SOCKS proxies, forward vs reverse proxies, and the limits of proxy anonymity.

22.about: Chapter 22 is the first hands-on anonymity exercise. AnonSurf becomes the vehicle for learning git clone: install Git, download the tool from its GitHub repository, read the README before running an installer, then start, stop and check the service and confirm whether your visible IP changed.
learn: What git clone does and how to download a tool from GitHub
How to install Git on Kali Linux if it is missing
What AnonSurf is and how it routes traffic through Tor
How to install, start, stop and check AnonSurf
How to verify whether your visible IP address changed
What AnonSurf cannot protect you from

concepts.p: Cloning a repository downloads code, and running its installer executes that code with your privileges. Always read the README, inspect the install script and check recent activity before running tools from GitHub, especially as root.

A tool reporting that it started is not proof that traffic is routed through Tor. Compare your public IP and check the Tor Project's detection page before and after enabling it, then disable it and confirm the original path returns.

practical.intro: Use a lab VM. Commands follow the workflow demonstrated in the chapter; the exact repository URL is shown in the video.

commands.c: sudo apt update && sudo apt install git
commands.d: Install Git if it is not already present.
Download the AnonSurf repository shown in the tutorial.
Read the documentation before installing anything.
Start routing through Tor, as demonstrated.
Check whether the service reports an active state.
Stop routing and restore normal networking.

practical.safety: Review installer scripts before running them with sudo. AnonSurf changes system routing; keep a VM snapshot so you can recover from misconfiguration.

faq.q: Does AnonSurf make me completely anonymous?
faq.a: No. It routes system traffic through Tor, which hides your IP from destinations, but identity leaks through logins, browser fingerprints and misconfiguration are still possible.

faq.q: Why is git clone used in this chapter?
faq.a: It is the standard way to download source code from GitHub and is a skill you will reuse for many security tools.

22.seo_title: AnonSurf on Kali Linux: Route Traffic Through Tor
22.seo_description: Install and use AnonSurf on Kali Linux: git clone, read the installer, start and stop Tor routing, and verify your public IP actually changed.

23.about: Chapter 23 explains what a VPN actually does. It covers the encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN server, why websites see the server's IP, how a VPN compares with a proxy, Tor and AnonSurf, the roles of OpenVPN, WireGuard and IPsec, and the protections a VPN does not provide.
learn: What a virtual private network is
How a VPN encrypts traffic and changes the IP address destinations see
How VPNs compare with proxies, Tor and AnonSurf
What OpenVPN, WireGuard and IPsec are at a high level
What a VPN does not protect against
Why VPN trust depends on the provider

concepts.p: A VPN client creates an encrypted connection to a VPN server. Traffic inside the tunnel is protected from the local network and the ISP, then exits to the internet from the VPN server. The destination sees the server's address, while the VPN provider can associate activity with your account.

OpenVPN is mature and widely supported, WireGuard is modern and lightweight, and IPsec is common in enterprise site-to-site deployments. Protocol choice affects performance, compatibility and configuration complexity more than it affects the basic privacy model.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and prepares you for the OpenVPN walkthrough in Chapter 24.
practical.safety: A VPN shifts trust to the provider. Choose providers with clear logging policies, and never assume a VPN authorizes any activity.

faq.q: Does a VPN make me anonymous?
faq.a: No. It hides your IP from destinations, but the VPN provider can still link traffic to your account, and browser or login identifiers can reveal you.

faq.q: VPN or Tor: which is better?
faq.a: They solve different problems. A VPN is simpler and faster for privacy from local networks; Tor is designed to resist traffic correlation but is slower and not a substitute for safe behaviour.

23.seo_title: What Is a VPN? How It Works vs Proxy and Tor
23.seo_description: Learn how a VPN works: the encrypted tunnel, how websites see the VPN server's IP, OpenVPN vs WireGuard vs IPsec, and what a VPN cannot protect.

24.about: Chapter 24 connects Kali to a VPN from the terminal. It shows what you need before starting, how to install OpenVPN, how to inspect a .ovpn configuration file, connect, verify your IP and DNS, troubleshoot common errors, and disconnect or switch servers. No VPN provider is recommended.
learn: What to check before choosing a VPN service
How to install OpenVPN on Kali Linux
How a .ovpn configuration file is structured
How to connect and disconnect from the terminal
How to verify your public IP and check for DNS leaks
How to diagnose common OpenVPN connection errors

concepts.p: An OpenVPN profile contains the remote server, protocol, port, certificates or key references and routing directives. Treat it as sensitive configuration: it may include credentials or private keys and should not be committed to a public repository.
After connecting, check that your public IP changed and that DNS queries resolve through the tunnel. A leaked DNS resolver can reveal the sites you visit even while web traffic uses the VPN.

practical.intro: Use a profile from a provider you trust and keep it outside the repository, for example in a directory excluded by .gitignore.

commands.c: sudo apt update && sudo apt install openvpn
commands.d: Install the OpenVPN client.
Connect using the profile. Keep the terminal open.
Check the public IP address in use.
Disconnect the foreground OpenVPN process.

practical.safety: Never share .ovpn files or embedded keys. Store profiles with restrictive permissions and keep them out of Git.

faq.q: Can I use any .ovpn file?
faq.a: Only one issued by a provider or administrator you trust. A profile points your traffic at a server, so an unknown profile can intercept it.

faq.q: Why does OpenVPN fail with a TLS error?
faq.a: Common causes include an expired profile, a wrong system clock, a blocked UDP port or a certificate mismatch. Check the client log for the first error rather than the last.

24.seo_title: How to Use OpenVPN on Kali Linux (.ovpn Setup)
24.seo_description: Connect Kali Linux to a VPN with OpenVPN: install the client, inspect a .ovpn profile, connect, verify your IP and DNS, disconnect safely and fix errors.

25.about: Chapter 25 separates Tor facts from dark-web myths. It defines the surface web, deep web and dark web, explains what Tor is, how onion routing passes traffic through relays, what .onion services are, and how Tor compares with a VPN or proxy. Legal and safety considerations close the lesson without linking to any hidden site.
learn: What Tor is and how traffic passes through several relays
The difference between the surface web, deep web and dark web
What .onion services are at a high level
How Tor compares with a VPN and a proxy
Common myths about Tor and the dark web
Legal and safety considerations when using Tor

concepts.p: The surface web is indexed by search engines. The deep web is content not indexed, such as private accounts and databases. The dark web is a small set of services reachable only through anonymity networks such as Tor. Using Tor is not itself illegal in most places; the legality of what you do remains unchanged.

Tor chooses a path of relays and encrypts traffic in layers so each relay knows only its predecessor and successor. No single relay sees both who you are and where you are going, which is the property the design is built around.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and deliberately shares no hidden-service links.
practical.safety: Do not explore illegal marketplaces or services. Tor is a privacy tool used by journalists, researchers and ordinary users, but it does not make unlawful activity lawful.

faq.q: Is using Tor illegal?
faq.a: In most countries, using Tor is legal. Laws target criminal activity, not the network itself. Check your local regulations if you are unsure.

faq.q: Can I be tracked on Tor?
faq.a: Tor resists network-level tracking, but logins, browser fingerprints, downloaded files and misconfigured applications can still reveal your identity.

25.seo_title: Is the Dark Web Illegal? How Tor Really Works
25.seo_description: Understand Tor without the myths: surface web vs deep web vs dark web, onion routing, .onion services, and the legal and safety facts beginners need.

26.about: Chapter 26 builds a harmless website and then publishes it as a Tor hidden service. It explains domains and servers, installs XAMPP, starts Apache, creates a test page, configures Tor to expose that local site as a .onion address, and tests it in Tor Browser. No real dark-web links are shared.
learn: What domains and servers do
How to install XAMPP and start Apache on Kali
How to host a basic page on localhost
How a Tor hidden service maps a local port to a .onion address
How to test the service in Tor Browser
How to avoid leaking identifying information through the service

concepts.p: A hidden service tells the Tor daemon to forward connections arriving at a .onion address to a local port, such as the Apache server on 127.0.0.1:80. The service's private key determines the address, so losing or exposing the key compromises the identity of the service.

A test page should contain no personal details, analytics, external fonts or images that reveal your clearnet infrastructure. Hidden services are a privacy technology, but they are only as private as the server configuration around them.

practical.intro: The lab uses XAMPP and Tor on your own VM. The exact Tor configuration is demonstrated step by step in the video.

commands.d: Run the XAMPP installer you downloaded from the official site.
Start Apache and the other XAMPP services.
Start the Tor service.
Review the hidden-service configuration before editing it.

practical.safety: Publish only a harmless test page, keep the service key private, and shut the service down after practice. Never expose personal data through a hidden service.

faq.q: Do I need a public IP to host a .onion site?
faq.a: No. Tor introduces circuits to your local service, so the machine does not need an inbound public address.

faq.q: Why does my .onion address change?
faq.a: The address is derived from the service's key. Regenerating the key produces a new address, so back up the original if you need it to stay stable.

26.seo_title: Host a .onion Website on Tor: XAMPP + Kali Linux Lab
26.seo_description: Host a harmless .onion test site in a lab: install XAMPP, run Apache, configure a Tor hidden service, find the address and test it in Tor Browser.

27.about: Chapter 27 explains onion routing step by step. It shows how traffic is wrapped in layers of encryption, what entry, middle and exit relays can each see, how .onion services differ from ordinary Tor browsing, and where Tor's practical and theoretical limits lie. No dark-web links are included.
learn: The problem Tor was designed to solve
How a request travels through three relays
Why each relay knows only its neighbours in the circuit
How layered encryption works at a high level
What an exit relay can see and why HTTPS still matters
How hidden services differ from normal Tor browsing
Where Tor's practical limits are

concepts.p: The entry relay knows your network address but not the destination. The middle relay knows neither end. The exit relay knows the destination and the unencrypted traffic if the site uses plain HTTP. End-to-end HTTPS protects content, while Tor protects the relationship between source and destination.

Tor does not protect you from logging into an identified account, downloading and opening documents that contact the network directly, or a compromised endpoint. Global adversaries who observe large parts of the network may also attempt traffic correlation.

practical.intro: This is the conceptual companion to the AnonSurf, Tor and Proxychains labs.
practical.safety: Tor Browser's default protections matter. Changing security settings or installing extensions can weaken the properties the design provides.

faq.q: Can the exit node see my traffic?
faq.a: It can see traffic to the destination if that traffic is unencrypted. HTTPS prevents the exit node from reading content, though it still sees the destination address.

faq.q: Does Tor hide the fact that I am using Tor?
faq.a: No. Your ISP or network operator can usually tell that you are connecting to Tor, even though they cannot see your destinations.

27.seo_title: How Tor Works: Entry, Middle and Exit Relays Explained
27.seo_description: A plain-language explanation of onion routing: how Tor wraps traffic in layers, what entry, middle and exit relays can see, and where Tor's limits are.

28.about: Chapter 28 routes individual tools through Tor with Proxychains. It explains how the wrapper intercepts connections, where the configuration file lives, how strict, dynamic and random chain modes differ, how to point Proxychains at Tor, how to run Nmap through it, and how to fix common errors.
learn: What Proxychains is and how traffic flows through its chain
Where the configuration file is and which lines matter
How strict, dynamic and random chain modes differ
How to point Proxychains at a local Tor SOCKS proxy
How to run a tool such as Nmap through the chain
How to troubleshoot common Proxychains errors

concepts.p: Proxychains hooks network calls in the program it launches and sends them to the configured proxies. It only affects programs started through it. Other traffic on the system keeps using the normal route unless you redirect it separately.

Strict mode uses every proxy in order and fails if one is unavailable. Dynamic mode tries proxies in sequence to establish a working chain. Random mode selects proxies randomly. For Tor, a single local SOCKS entry on port 9050 is the usual configuration.

practical.intro: Edit the configuration only after backing it up, and test with a harmless request before using security tools.

commands.d: Back up the configuration first.
Review chain mode and the proxy list.
Ensure Tor is running for the SOCKS entry.
Test whether requests use the Tor circuit.
Run a TCP connect scan through the chain in your lab.

practical.safety: Proxychains can break tools that use raw packets, UDP or their own network stack. Scan only your own lab; routing does not grant authorization.

faq.q: Why does Nmap fail through Proxychains?
faq.a: SYN scans and raw-packet features do not translate cleanly to a SOCKS proxy. Use TCP connect scans with -sT and expect reduced accuracy.

faq.q: Does Proxychains apply to my whole system?
faq.a: No. It only affects processes launched through the proxychains command.

28.seo_title: Proxychains in Kali Linux: Route Tools Through Tor
28.seo_description: Configure Proxychains to send tool traffic through Tor: edit proxychains4.conf, choose a chain mode, test the circuit, and understand Nmap limitations.

29.about: Chapter 29 combines the previous two lessons into a complete Tor plus Proxychains workflow. It demonstrates the correct order to start services, the configuration that keeps tools inside the Tor circuit, how to confirm traffic leaves through an exit node rather than your real address, and the common mistakes that silently break the chain.
learn: How Tor and Proxychains fit together in practice
The correct order for starting Tor and testing the chain
How to verify that traffic really uses a Tor exit node
Which configuration mistakes silently bypass Tor
How to recover when the chain stops working
Why wrapping a tool is not the same as system-wide anonymity

concepts.p: Tor must be running before a wrapped tool attempts a connection. If the SOCKS port is closed, a permissive Proxychains configuration may fall back to a direct connection, which defeats the purpose. Verify Tor status, then test the chain with a simple request.

Check your public address from inside the wrapped command, not from a separate browser. DNS resolution, IPv6 traffic and tools that bypass the wrapper are common leak paths, so a single IP check is a starting point rather than a full audit.

practical.intro: Follow the order shown in the tutorial and confirm each step before running a security tool.

commands.d: Start the Tor service.
Confirm the service is active.
Check the address seen when traffic passes through the chain.
Confirm the request is using Tor.

practical.safety: Do not assume success from a tool banner. Verify the exit path, and remember that authorization to test a system is independent of how you route traffic.

faq.q: Why does my real IP still appear with Proxychains?
faq.a: Tor may not be running, the proxy entry may be wrong, or the tool may bypass the wrapper. Check the service, the port and the tool's networking behaviour.

faq.q: Is Proxychains plus Tor enough for anonymity?
faq.a: No. It only covers wrapped processes. Browser fingerprinting, logins, DNS and unencrypted traffic can still expose you.

29.seo_title: Tor + Proxychains in Kali Linux: Step-by-Step Setup
29.seo_description: Combine Tor and Proxychains correctly: start services in order, verify traffic uses an exit node, avoid silent bypasses and troubleshoot common failures.

30.about: Chapter 30 introduces MAC address spoofing with macchanger. It explains what a MAC address is, how it differs from an IP address, why it can be used to track a device on a local network, and demonstrates setting a random or custom address and restoring the original. The privacy and authorized-testing context is made explicit.
learn: What a MAC address is and how it differs from an IP address
Why MAC addresses can be used for tracking or access control
How to change to a random MAC with macchanger
How to set a specific MAC address
How to restore the original hardware address
The legal and ethical limits of MAC spoofing

concepts.p: A MAC address identifies a network interface on the local segment. It is used by switches and wireless access points, while IP addresses handle routing across networks. Captive portals, hotel networks and some access controls key on MAC addresses, which is why changing one can bypass simplistic restrictions.
MAC spoofing changes the address the operating system presents, not the burned-in hardware address. It lasts until reboot or until you restore it. Record the original address before changing it.

practical.intro: Use your own lab interface. Replace eth0 with your actual interface name from ip link.

commands.d: Identify the interface and its current MAC address.

commands.c: sudo ip link set eth0 down
commands.d: Bring the interface down before changing its address.
Assign a random MAC address.

commands.c: sudo ip link set eth0 up
commands.d: Bring the interface back up.
Restore the original hardware address (interface down first).

practical.safety: Changing a MAC does not authorize access to a network. Bypassing access controls can violate policy or law, even on a network you can physically reach.

faq.q: Does changing my MAC address hide me on the internet?
faq.a: No. It only changes your layer-2 identity on the local network. Destinations still see your public IP address.

faq.q: Why does macchanger fail with 'interface is up'?
faq.a: The interface must be down while the address changes. Run ip link set <interface> down, change the MAC, then bring it back up.

30.seo_title: Change Your MAC Address in Kali Linux (macchanger)
30.seo_description: Learn MAC address spoofing in Kali Linux with macchanger: what a MAC address is, random and custom addresses, restoring the original, and legal limits.

31.about: Chapter 31 is the complete macchanger reference. It demonstrates checking the current address, setting a random address, keeping the same vendor, setting a custom value, restoring the original, and fixing the common interface-is-up error. It is designed so you stop copying a single command from memory.
learn: How to display the current and permanent MAC address
How to set a fully random MAC address
How to generate a random address that keeps the same vendor prefix
How to set a specific custom MAC address
How to restore the permanent hardware address
How to fix interface-state errors

concepts.p: The first three bytes of a MAC address identify the vendor (the OUI). A fully random address may look like an unknown device, while a same-vendor random address blends in with other hardware from that manufacturer. Both are presentation choices, not anonymity guarantees.
Most failures come from trying to change an address on an interface that is up, or from using the wrong interface name. Bring it down, change the address, verify, then bring it up.

practical.intro: Check each option against your own interface in a lab VM.

commands.d: Show the current and permanent MAC address.
Set a random MAC address.
Set a random address within the same vendor range.
Set a specific custom address.
Restore the permanent address.

practical.safety: Some networks enforce MAC-based policies. Bypassing them can breach acceptable-use rules or law. Use spoofing for privacy and authorized testing.

faq.q: What does macchanger -A do?
faq.a: It sets a random MAC address while keeping the same vendor prefix as the original interface.

faq.q: Does the change survive a reboot?
faq.a: No. MAC changes are temporary unless you configure them to run at boot, which is not recommended for normal use.

31.seo_title: macchanger Commands: Every Option Explained (Kali Linux)
31.seo_description: A complete macchanger reference for Kali Linux: show, random, same-vendor, custom, restore and troubleshoot the interface-is-up error.

32.about: Chapter 32 begins the ethical hacking methodology with footprinting, the information-gathering phase that happens before any active testing. It separates passive from active footprinting, shows what kinds of information are collected, and explains where that information comes from and why it shapes every later phase.
learn: What footprinting is and where it fits in a penetration test
The difference between passive and active footprinting
What information is collected about an organization
Which public sources reveal domain, infrastructure and people data
How footprinting feeds scanning, enumeration and exploitation
Why scope and authorization must be defined first

concepts.p: Passive footprinting uses public information without touching the target: search engines, social media, public records, certificate transparency and DNS history. It is quiet and low risk. Active footprinting sends traffic to target systems and must stay inside an authorized scope.

A penetration test starts with a written scope that lists allowed targets, time windows and prohibited techniques. Footprinting often reveals related domains and third parties; discovering them does not authorize testing them.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual. It establishes the methodology used by every reconnaissance tool that follows.
practical.safety: Collect only public information and stay inside the agreed scope. Active probing of systems you do not own or have permission to test is unauthorized access.

faq.q: What is the difference between footprinting and scanning?
faq.a: Footprinting gathers information from public and semi-public sources. Scanning actively probes systems to discover hosts, ports and services.

faq.q: Is footprinting legal?
faq.a: Using public sources is generally legal. Active footprinting and any testing of target systems require authorization.

32.seo_title: What Is Footprinting? First Step of Ethical Hacking
32.seo_description: Footprinting explained: passive vs active reconnaissance, what information is collected, where it comes from, and how it feeds scanning and enumeration.

33.about: Chapter 33 moves from footprinting concepts to DNS reconnaissance. It explains what DNS enumeration is, which records matter during an assessment, and how to query them manually with dig and nslookup before moving to automated Kali tools. Subdomains, mail servers and name servers are the focus.
learn: What DNS enumeration is and why it matters in reconnaissance
Which DNS record types reveal useful infrastructure details
How to query records with dig
How to use nslookup for basic lookups
How subdomains, MX and NS records expand the attack surface
How to stay inside an authorized scope while enumerating

concepts.h: DNS is a map of the organization
concepts.p: A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT and CNAME records reveal where services live, who handles mail, which name servers are authoritative and which third parties are involved. TXT records can also expose verification tokens and mail security policy.
Running dig and nslookup by hand teaches you what the automated tools are doing and helps you validate their output. It also produces evidence you can explain in a report.

practical.intro: Query a domain you own or a public example domain; do not enumerate third parties without permission.

commands.d: Resolve the domain's IPv4 address.
List mail exchangers for the domain.
List authoritative name servers.
Show TXT records such as SPF and verification entries.
Perform a simple forward lookup.

practical.safety: DNS enumeration generates queries that can be logged. Enumerate only domains you own or are authorized to assess.

faq.q: What is the difference between dig and nslookup?
faq.a: Both query DNS. dig provides more detailed output and is preferred for troubleshooting and scripting, while nslookup is simpler and available on many platforms.

faq.q: Which DNS record reveals mail servers?
faq.a: MX records list the mail exchangers responsible for accepting email for the domain.

33.seo_title: DNS Enumeration in Kali Linux: dig, nslookup & Records
33.seo_description: Learn DNS enumeration with dig and nslookup: read A, AAAA, MX, NS and TXT records, map a domain's infrastructure and understand reconnaissance scope.

34.about: Chapter 34 automates the manual DNS work from the previous lesson with Dnsenum. It shows how to run the tool against a domain, how it uses wordlists to find subdomains, how to read the output, and how to combine it with other reconnaissance data.
learn: How Dnsenum automates DNS enumeration
How to run Dnsenum against an authorized domain
How subdomain discovery uses wordlists
How to read name server, mail and host records in the output
How to combine Dnsenum results with manual dig queries
Why noisy enumeration needs rate and scope control

concepts.p: Dnsenum performs record lookups, zone-transfer attempts (where allowed) and subdomain brute force with a wordlist. The wordlist determines which names are tried, so a focused list is usually more useful than a massive generic one.
Automated output can contain stale records and false positives. Confirm interesting hosts with dig or a direct connection before treating them as live parts of the target's infrastructure.

practical.intro: Use a domain you own. The tool is available in Kali by default.

commands.d: Run a default enumeration against an authorized domain.
Run the more complete enumeration preset.
Use a specific subdomain wordlist.

practical.safety: Subdomain brute forcing creates many DNS requests and may trigger alerts. Only enumerate domains you own or have written permission to test.

faq.q: Does Dnsenum perform zone transfers?
faq.a: It attempts them and reports the result. Most correctly configured name servers refuse unauthorized transfers.

faq.q: Why are some discovered subdomains unreachable?
faq.a: DNS records can point to retired, internal or unresponsive hosts. Verify each candidate before drawing conclusions.

34.seo_title: Dnsenum Tutorial: Find Subdomains Automatically in Kali
34.seo_description: Use Dnsenum in Kali Linux to automate DNS enumeration: run it against an authorized domain, read the output, and find subdomains with wordlists.

35.about: Chapter 35 adds DNSmap to the enumeration toolkit. It explains how wordlist-driven subdomain discovery works, runs DNSmap against a test domain, compares it with Dnsenum, and shows how to read the output. The wordlist concept carries forward to password attacks later in the course.
learn: How DNSmap uses wordlists to enumerate subdomains
How to run DNSmap against an authorized domain
How to read discovered hostnames and addresses
How DNSmap differs from Dnsenum
Why wordlist quality affects results
How to confirm discovered hosts

concepts.p: DNSmap prepends candidate labels from a wordlist to the target domain and queries DNS for each. A hit means the name resolves, not necessarily that it hosts a live or interesting service. The technique is simple and still effective because organizations forget old names.

The same candidate names used for subdomain discovery often reappear in virtual-host discovery, content discovery and password guessing. Building a curated list for a target type is a skill that compounds across engagements.

practical.intro: Run DNSmap only against domains you own or are authorized to test.

commands.d: Run a default subdomain scan with the built-in wordlist.
Use a custom wordlist of candidate labels.
Save the results to a file for review.

practical.safety: High-volume DNS queries are visible to the target and its DNS provider. Keep request rates reasonable and respect scope.

faq.q: What is the difference between DNSmap and Dnsenum?
faq.a: Both enumerate DNS. Dnsenum bundles record lookups and zone-transfer attempts with brute forcing; DNSmap focuses on wordlist-driven subdomain discovery.

faq.q: What wordlist should I start with?
faq.a: The built-in list in Kali is a reasonable start. A smaller, target-relevant list often produces cleaner results than a huge generic list.

35.seo_title: DNSmap Tutorial: Find Subdomains with Wordlists
35.seo_description: Learn DNSmap in Kali Linux: wordlist-driven subdomain discovery, custom wordlists, reading results, and how it differs from Dnsenum.

36.about: Chapter 36 covers DNStracer, which follows a DNS query from the root servers through the TLD to the authoritative name server. It explains how to read that path, why it is useful during reconnaissance, and how it complements the subdomain tools from the previous two chapters.
learn: What DNStracer does differently from subdomain discovery tools
How a DNS query travels from root to authoritative servers
How to run DNStracer against a domain
How to read the delegation path in the output
When tracing DNS is useful during reconnaissance
How DNStracer fits with Dnsenum and DNSmap

concepts.p: Resolving a name starts at a root server, which refers the resolver to the relevant TLD servers, which refer it to the domain's authoritative servers. DNStracer displays these hops, making misconfigurations and unusual hosting arrangements visible.

Understanding which provider hosts a domain's DNS can reveal shared infrastructure or outsourcing relationships. That context helps interpret other findings and avoid testing infrastructure outside scope.

practical.intro: Trace a domain you own or a public example domain.

commands.d: Trace the DNS resolution path for the domain.
Start the trace explicitly from a root server.
Show more detail about each hop.

practical.safety: Tracing sends queries to public DNS infrastructure. Keep queries modest and never attempt zone transfers against domains you do not own.

faq.q: Does DNStracer find subdomains?
faq.a: No. It traces how a specific name resolves through the DNS hierarchy. Use Dnsenum or DNSmap for subdomain discovery.

faq.q: Why does the trace show a third-party provider?
faq.a: Many organizations delegate DNS to a hosting or CDN provider. That delegation is useful context for mapping infrastructure.

36.seo_title: DNStracer Tutorial: Trace DNS Resolution in Kali Linux
36.seo_description: Trace DNS resolution with DNStracer: follow a query from root to TLD to authoritative servers, read the delegation path, and use it during recon.

37.about: Chapter 37 prepares you to scan by first understanding your own network. It shows how to find your IP and MAC address with ifconfig and the modern ip a command, how to read the routing table and default gateway with route -n, what Nmap is, and how to run a first scan against your own lab network.
learn: Why understanding your own network comes before scanning
How to find interface addresses with ifconfig and ip a
How to read a routing table and identify the default gateway
What Nmap does and why it is central to reconnaissance
How to run a basic host-discovery scan in a lab
Which scanning mistakes cause confusion or scope violations

concepts.p: Your interface address, subnet mask and default gateway define what your machine can reach directly. Without them, scan results are hard to interpret and you may accidentally probe a network outside your lab.

A ping sweep such as nmap -sn identifies live hosts without scanning ports. Starting here narrows the target list and reduces unnecessary traffic, which matters for both performance and authorization.

practical.intro: Run these inside your lab VM and confirm the results match your virtual network settings.

commands.d: Show interfaces and addresses (modern replacement for ifconfig).
Show interface details if net-tools is installed.
Display the routing table and default gateway.
Discover live hosts in your own lab subnet without port scanning.

practical.safety: Scan only your own lab or systems you have written permission to test. A ping sweep of a public or corporate network can violate policy and law.

faq.q: What is the difference between ifconfig and ip a?
