faq.a: Both show interface information. ip a is part of the modern iproute2 suite and is available by default on current Linux systems; ifconfig comes from the older net-tools package.

faq.q: What is a default gateway?
faq.a: The router your machine sends traffic to when the destination is not on the local subnet.

37.seo_title: Nmap for Beginners: Check Your Network First
37.seo_description: Before scanning with Nmap, learn your own network: ip a and ifconfig for addresses, route -n for the gateway, then a safe first host-discovery scan in your lab.

38.about: Chapter 38 teaches the core Nmap workflow. It covers basic syntax, scanning a single host and a range, the -sS, -sT and -sU scan types, selecting ports, service and version detection with -sV, OS detection with -O, saving output to a file, and reading the results.
learn: How to write a basic Nmap command for one host
How to scan a network range responsibly
The difference between SYN, TCP connect and UDP scans
How to scan specific ports versus the full range
How service and version detection work with -sV
How to use -O and save results to a file

concepts.p: A SYN scan (-sS) sends a TCP SYN and infers state from the reply without completing the handshake; it usually needs root. A TCP connect scan (-sT) completes the handshake, works without raw sockets and is easier to log. A UDP scan (-sU) sends UDP probes and is slow because many services do not reply.

Nmap's default scan covers the 1000 most common TCP ports. -p selects specific ports and -p- covers all 65535. -sV probes open ports to identify the service and version, which is what turns a list of open ports into useful reconnaissance.

practical.intro: Use a lab target such as a Metasploitable VM. Replace addresses and ports with your own lab values.

commands.d: Scan the 1000 most common TCP ports on one host.
Scan a lab subnet.
Run a SYN scan (root required).
Run a TCP connect scan without raw sockets.
Scan selected UDP ports.
Detect service versions on chosen ports.
Attempt operating system detection.
Save normal-format output to a file.

practical.safety: A full-port or UDP scan can be slow and noisy. Scan only authorized lab systems, and avoid -p- or aggressive timing on networks you do not control.

faq.q: What is the difference between -sS and -sT?
faq.a: -sS uses a half-open SYN scan and usually requires root. -sT completes the TCP handshake and works as a normal user, but is easier for the target to log.

faq.q: Why is a UDP scan so slow?
faq.a: Many UDP services do not respond to probes, so Nmap must wait for timeouts to decide a port is open|filtered.

38.seo_title: Nmap Scan Types Explained: -sS vs -sT vs -sU
38.seo_description: Learn Nmap scanning: basic syntax, host ranges, -sS vs -sT vs -sU, port selection, -sV service detection, -O OS detection and saving output.

39.about: Chapter 39 looks under the hood of Nmap. It explains what the tool sends and how port states are decided, then demonstrates ACK, FIN and Xmas scans, timing templates -T0 through -T5, the aggressive -A option, output formats -oN, -oX, -oG and -oA, and the first steps with the Nmap Scripting Engine.
learn: What Nmap sends and how it decides a port is open, closed or filtered
What ACK, FIN and Xmas scans are used for
How timing options -T0 to -T5 affect speed and visibility
What the aggressive -A scan combines
How to save output in normal, XML, grepable and combined formats
How to run a basic NSE script

concepts.p: Nmap interprets replies, or the absence of replies. Open means a service accepted the probe, closed means the host replied with a rejection, and filtered usually means a firewall dropped the packet. A filtered result is not proof that no service exists.

Timing templates trade speed for reliability and stealth. -T4 is common on fast, reliable lab networks. Higher templates send more aggressively and are more likely to overwhelm weak services or trigger defences.

practical.intro: Practise on your own lab host and compare how each option changes output and runtime.

commands.d: ACK scan to probe firewall filtering behaviour.
FIN scan, which may bypass some simple filters.
Xmas scan with FIN, PSH and URG flags set.
Use an aggressive-but-reasonable timing template in a lab.
Enable OS detection, version detection, scripts and traceroute.
Save normal, XML and grepable output with one base name.
Run a single NSE script against a web port.

practical.safety: -A and NSE scripts are noisy and can be intrusive. Do not run them against production systems without explicit authorization and a change window.

faq.q: What does the -A flag do?
faq.a: It enables several detections at once: OS detection, version detection, script scanning and traceroute. It is powerful but noisy.

faq.q: What is the Nmap Scripting Engine?
faq.a: NSE runs Lua scripts that extend Nmap for tasks such as service discovery, enumeration and basic vulnerability checks.

39.seo_title: Nmap ACK, FIN, Xmas Scans and NSE Explained
39.seo_description: Go deeper with Nmap: ACK, FIN and Xmas scans, -T0 to -T5 timing, the -A aggressive scan, output formats -oN -oX -oG -oA, and NSE basics.

40.about: Chapter 40 connects scanning to vulnerability research. After Nmap reveals a service and version, Searchsploit searches the local Exploit-DB archive for documented issues in that software. The lesson covers searching by name and version, reading results, filtering, viewing and copying an entry, updating the database, and where this fits in a penetration test.
learn: What Searchsploit and Exploit-DB are
How to search by software name and version
How to read and filter search results
How to view an exploit entry and copy it to a working directory
How to update the local Exploit-DB archive
Why a public exploit match is not proof of exploitability

concepts.p: Searchsploit queries a local copy of Exploit-DB, so it works without sending requests to the target. It is a research aid: results describe documented vulnerabilities, not confirmation that your specific target is vulnerable.

A version banner can be inaccurate, backported patches can remove a vulnerability, and exploit code may be unreliable or destructive. Validation in an isolated lab comes before any exploitation, and exploitation requires authorization.

practical.intro: Search using a version you found in your own lab scan, then inspect the entry without running it.

commands.d: Search the local archive for matching software.
Search titles only for a narrower result set.
Perform an exact match search.
Copy an exploit entry into the current directory by EDB ID.
Update the local Exploit-DB archive.

practical.safety: Downloaded exploit code may be malicious, broken or destructive. Read it before running it, test only in a snapshot-protected lab, and never against systems without authorization.

faq.q: Does Searchsploit test my target?
faq.a: No. It searches a local database of documented exploits. You still have to validate whether the target is affected.

faq.q: How do I update Exploit-DB?
faq.a: Run sudo searchsploit --update, which refreshes the local archive from the Exploit-DB repository.

40.seo_title: Searchsploit Tutorial: Find Exploits for Nmap Results
40.seo_description: Use Searchsploit to turn Nmap service versions into vulnerability research: search Exploit-DB, filter results, inspect entries, update the database and stay legal.

41.about: Chapter 41 profiles a website before testing it. It explains website footprinting, then uses WhatWeb to identify technologies, Whois to read domain registration details and Dirb to discover directories and files. The lesson closes by showing how the three tools answer different questions about the same target.
learn: What website footprinting is and why it precedes testing
How WhatWeb identifies CMS, frameworks and server technologies
How Whois reveals registration and ownership details
How Dirb performs content discovery with wordlists
How to read and cross-check results from each tool
Why discovered paths require authorization before access

concepts.p: WhatWeb answers what the site runs, Whois answers who registered the domain and when, and Dirb answers which paths exist. Together they build a profile that guides later testing without sending exploit traffic.
Dirb requests many candidate paths. Results include redirects, soft-404 pages and false positives, so verify interesting findings with a normal request and record status codes and response sizes.

practical.intro: Use your own lab web app or a site you have written permission to assess.

commands.d: Fingerprint web technologies.
Read domain registration details.
Discover common paths with a wordlist.
Save content-discovery results to a file.

practical.safety: Content discovery can generate thousands of requests and trigger blocking. Only scan sites you own or are explicitly authorized to test, and keep request rates modest.

faq.q: What is the difference between WhatWeb and Dirb?
faq.a: WhatWeb identifies the technologies a site uses. Dirb looks for existing paths and files using a wordlist.

faq.q: Is Whois information public?
faq.a: Registration data is published through Whois, although privacy services may mask personal details.

41.seo_title: WhatWeb, Whois and Dirb: Website Recon in Kali Linux
41.seo_description: Profile a website before testing: WhatWeb technology fingerprinting, Whois domain details and Dirb content discovery, with responsible-use guidance.

42.about: Chapter 42 introduces vulnerability analysis with Nikto. It explains how scanning differs from exploitation, runs Nikto against an owned test site, demonstrates options for ports, SSL and output files, and then focuses on reading results, recognising false positives and prioritising findings.
learn: What a Nikto scan can and cannot tell you
How vulnerability analysis differs from exploitation
How to run a first Nikto scan against a lab site
How to select ports, enable SSL checks and save output
How to separate real findings from false positives
How to prioritise remediation work

concepts.p: Nikto sends requests and compares responses against a large database of known files, headers and misconfigurations. It reports potential issues, not proof of exploitability. Confirming impact is a separate, authorized step.

A long Nikto report is not a long list of urgent problems. Prioritise exposed administrative interfaces, outdated components with known exploits, sensitive files and missing security headers in that order, and verify each item manually.

practical.intro: Target an intentionally vulnerable lab app such as DVWA or a test server you control.

commands.d: Scan a lab web server on the default port.
Force SSL/TLS checking.
Scan a non-standard port.
Save the report to a file.

practical.safety: Nikto is noisy and can be blocked or alert defenders. Use it only on lab systems or with written authorization, and never against shared hosting without permission.

faq.q: Does Nikto exploit vulnerabilities?
faq.a: No. It performs non-intrusive checks and reports potential issues. Exploitation is a separate phase that requires explicit authorization.

faq.q: Why does Nikto report outdated software that is actually patched?
faq.a: It often relies on banners and headers. Backported patches can leave version strings unchanged, so verify the finding manually.

42.seo_title: Nikto Tutorial: Scan a Web Server for Vulnerabilities
42.seo_description: Learn Nikto web server scanning: how vulnerability analysis differs from exploitation, port and SSL options, reading results and prioritising real findings.

43.about: Chapter 43 explains cross-site scripting without turning the lesson into a payload dump. It covers why the browser trusts the page, the difference between reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS, real impact such as session theft and page defacement, a safe practice-app demonstration, and the defences developers use.
learn: What cross-site scripting is and why it happens
The difference between reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS
What an attacker can achieve with script execution in a browser
How to test for XSS safely in an owned lab application
How output encoding, input handling and CSP reduce risk
Why XSS is a developer problem as much as a tester's finding

concepts.p: Reflected XSS bounces input straight back in a response. Stored XSS persists input, such as a comment, and affects every viewer. DOM-based XSS occurs when client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page without safe handling.

Output must be encoded for the context where it appears: HTML body, attribute, URL or script. Input validation helps but is not sufficient. Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies and framework auto-escaping reduce impact and likelihood.

practical.intro: The demonstration uses an intentionally vulnerable practice app on your own VM. No attack payloads are reproduced here.
practical.safety: Never test XSS on a site you do not own or have written permission to assess. Stored XSS can affect other users, so even a lab test should stay isolated.

faq.q: Is XSS dangerous if the site has no login?
faq.a: Yes. Script execution can still redirect users, alter content, mine data in the page, or attack visitors through their browsers.

faq.q: Does a web application firewall fix XSS?
faq.a: A WAF can reduce some attacks but is not a substitute for correct output encoding. Bypasses are common.

43.seo_title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) for Beginners: How It Works
43.seo_description: Understand XSS: reflected, stored and DOM-based cross-site scripting, real impact, safe lab testing, and how developers prevent it with encoding and CSP.

44.about: Chapter 44 introduces RedHawk, a script that bundles several website reconnaissance checks. It shows how to install it with git clone, read the README and script before running it, execute it against an owned test site, interpret the server, Whois, geo-IP and CMS modules, and compare the results with separate tools.
learn: What RedHawk bundles into one reconnaissance workflow
How to install a GitHub-hosted tool with git clone
Why reading the README and source before running matters
How to interpret server, Whois, geo-IP and CMS output
What the built-in basic vulnerability checks can and cannot confirm
When separate tools give better control than an all-in-one script

concepts.p: All-in-one tools save typing but hide how each check works. You learn more by running WhatWeb, Whois and Nikto separately at least once, then using an aggregator when you understand what it is summarising.

Cloning and running a script executes someone else's code. Review the repository, check for recent maintenance and avoid running unknown scripts as root. The same discipline applies to every tool you install from GitHub.

practical.intro: Install in a lab VM and run it only against your own test site.

commands.d: Clone the repository shown in the tutorial.
Enter the cloned directory.
Read the instructions before running anything.
Run a scan against an authorized test site.

practical.safety: Do not run unreviewed scripts with sudo. Confirm the repository source, and scan only sites you own or have written permission to test.

faq.q: Is RedHawk a replacement for Nmap?
faq.a: No. It focuses on website reconnaissance and basic checks, not full network and port scanning.

faq.q: Why run separate tools if RedHawk does the same?
faq.a: Separate tools give clearer output, better control and a deeper understanding of each check. Aggregators are convenient once you know what they do.

44.seo_title: RedHawk Tutorial: All-in-One Website Recon Tool
44.seo_description: Use RedHawk for website reconnaissance: install with git clone, review the source, run server, Whois, geo-IP and CMS checks, and compare it with dedicated tools.

45.about: Chapter 45 switches to defence with a Linux security audit. It walks through the areas worth checking — users, groups and sudo, file permissions, running services and open ports, packages and updates — shows built-in commands for each, then demonstrates Lynis as an automated auditing tool and how to read its report.
learn: What a Linux security audit evaluates
How to review users, groups and sudo privileges
How to find weak file permissions
How to list running services and open ports
How to check package and update status
How to run Lynis and interpret its findings

concepts.p: Unnecessary services, world-writable files, weak sudo rules and stale packages are common weaknesses. An audit inventories what is running and who can change it, which is the same information an attacker uses after access.
Lynis produces a hardening index and many suggestions. The score is less important than the specific findings: critical exposures first, then configuration hardening, then informational advice.

practical.intro: Audit your own VM. Review each finding before changing anything.

commands.d: Show sudo permissions for your account.
List SUID binaries on the root filesystem.
Show listening TCP and UDP sockets with processes.
List packages with available updates.
Run a full local system audit.

practical.safety: Auditing is read-only, but remediation changes can break services. Apply fixes one at a time and keep a snapshot.

faq.q: What does the Lynis hardening index mean?
faq.a: It is a rough score of how well the system follows hardening guidance. It helps track progress but is not a certification or a guarantee of security.

faq.q: Should I run a security audit on someone else's server?
faq.a: Only with authorization. Even read-only checks can expose sensitive configuration and may violate policy or law without permission.

45.seo_title: Linux Security Audit with Lynis: Find Weak Spots
45.seo_description: Audit your Linux system: review users, sudo, permissions, services, ports and updates, then run Lynis and interpret the report to prioritise hardening.

46.about: Chapter 46 is a complete SQL injection lab. It explains what SQL injection is, why it happens, sets up DVWA as a practice target, runs a first SQLMap test, shows how to read the results and the real impact, and finishes with the developer defences that actually prevent it.
learn: What SQL injection is and why it happens
How SQLMap detects an injectable parameter
How to set up DVWA as a safe practice target
How to read SQLMap's output and enumerate databases
What real-world impact SQL injection can have
How parameterised queries and least privilege prevent it

concepts.p: SQL injection occurs when user input is concatenated into a query so the database treats part of the input as SQL syntax. Parameterised queries keep data and code separate, which is the primary fix.

SQLMap sends crafted requests, compares responses and identifies injection techniques. Because it can generate heavy traffic and extract data, it belongs only in a lab or an explicitly authorized engagement.

practical.intro: All demos target DVWA on your own VM. Replace the URL, cookie and parameters with your lab values.

commands.d: Test a lab parameter with the session cookie.
Accept default answers for automation.
Enumerate databases after confirming injection.
List tables in a specific database.

practical.safety: SQLMap can damage or overload a database and is illegal to use without authorization. Keep DVWA on a host-only lab network and take a snapshot first.

faq.q: How do developers prevent SQL injection?
faq.a: Use parameterised queries or an ORM, enforce least-privilege database accounts, hide detailed errors, and validate input as defence in depth.

faq.q: Can SQLMap test any website?
faq.a: Technically it can send requests, but doing so without permission is unauthorized access. Only test your own lab or systems within a written scope.

46.seo_title: SQLMap Tutorial: Test SQL Injection in a Safe Lab
46.seo_description: Learn SQL injection with SQLMap in a DVWA lab: how detection works, reading output, enumerating databases, real-world impact and developer defences.

47.about: Chapter 47 continues the SQL injection section with jSQL Injection, a graphical Java-based tool. It compares jSQL with SQLMap, tours the interface, tests a lab URL, enumerates databases, tables and columns visually, extracts data, and discusses when a GUI is more practical than a command-line workflow.
learn: What jSQL Injection is and how it differs from SQLMap
How to launch and navigate the jSQL interface
How to test a lab URL for SQL injection using the GUI
How to enumerate databases, tables and columns visually
How to extract data through the interface in a lab
The trade-offs between GUI and command-line SQL injection tools

concepts.p: jSQL and SQLMap both automate injection discovery and data extraction. The GUI makes the workflow visible, which helps beginners understand each stage, while SQLMap is easier to script and reproduce.

Point-and-click does not remove the need to define scope, confirm the target, capture evidence and stop before extracting more data than necessary. A GUI can make destructive actions feel harmless, so slow down.

practical.intro: jSQL Injection is included in Kali and is launched from the application menu. The video demonstrates the interface fields and workflow.
practical.safety: Use only against DVWA or another intentionally vulnerable app in an isolated lab. Automated extraction can be disruptive and is illegal without authorization.

faq.q: Is jSQL better than SQLMap?
faq.a: Neither is universally better. jSQL is more visual and beginner-friendly; SQLMap is more scriptable and widely used in professional workflows.

faq.q: Does jSQL require Java?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Java application, and Kali packages the necessary runtime with the tool.

47.seo_title: jSQL Injection Tutorial: GUI SQL Injection Testing
47.seo_description: Use jSQL Injection to test SQL injection visually: interface tour, database and table enumeration, data extraction in a lab, and how it compares with SQLMap.

48.about: Chapter 48 completes the SQL injection tool trio with sqlsus, a MySQL-focused interactive tool. It explains how sqlsus differs from SQLMap and jSQL, how to start it with a target configuration, how its interactive shell enumerates and extracts data, and when a MySQL-specific workflow is useful.
learn: What sqlsus is and how it differs from SQLMap and jSQL
Why sqlsus focuses on MySQL injection scenarios
How a sqlsus target configuration is structured
How the interactive shell enumerates databases and tables
How data extraction works in the tool
When to choose sqlsus over the alternatives

concepts.h: Three approaches to the same vulnerability class
concepts.p: SQLMap is command-line and highly automated, jSQL is graphical, and sqlsus offers an interactive shell with a MySQL focus. Learning multiple interfaces builds a mental model of the underlying technique rather than dependence on one tool.

sqlsus separates target details into a configuration file before opening its shell. That structure makes repeatable tests easier, but it also means the configuration must be accurate and scoped to an authorized lab target.

practical.intro: This chapter is scheduled for release; the exact commands are demonstrated in the video. Use only DVWA or another intentionally vulnerable MySQL app in an isolated lab.
practical.safety: Injection tools can modify or delete data. Work from a snapshot, use a dedicated lab database account, and never test without written authorization.

faq.q: Is sqlsus still maintained?
faq.a: It is an older, specialised tool. Check the version packaged in Kali and prefer actively maintained options for production engagements.

faq.q: Why learn a third SQL injection tool?
faq.a: Different interfaces expose different parts of the workflow. Understanding the technique matters more than memorising one tool's flags.

48.seo_title: sqlsus Tutorial: MySQL Injection and Exploitation Tool
48.seo_description: Explore sqlsus, a MySQL-focused SQL injection tool: configuration, interactive shell, data extraction, and how it compares with SQLMap and jSQL Injection.

49.about: Chapter 49 opens the password attack section with vocabulary and threat modelling. It defines password attacks, explains why credentials remain a weak point, compares brute force, dictionary, rainbow table and credential stuffing, separates online from offline attacks, introduces hashing and wordlists, and previews the tools used in the following chapters.
learn: What a password attack is and why credentials remain a common target
How brute force, dictionary, rainbow table and credential stuffing differ
The difference between online and offline password attacks
Why passwords are stored as hashes and why attackers target them
Why wordlists are central to most password attacks
Which tools the following chapters will demonstrate

concepts.p: An online attack guesses against a live service and is limited by network latency, rate limits and account lockouts. An offline attack guesses against captured hashes at local hardware speed, which is why a stolen hash database is far more dangerous than a login form.

Passwords remain the most common authentication factor. Reuse, weak patterns and breached credentials make them valuable even when systems use modern hashing, because attackers can try known passwords against many accounts.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and sets up the hands-on labs that follow.
practical.safety: Password attacks against systems you do not own are illegal. Test only your own lab accounts and never use credentials from breach dumps against real services.

faq.q: Which is faster: online or offline cracking?
faq.a: Offline cracking is usually much faster because there is no network round trip, rate limit or lockout. Speed depends on hash type and hardware.

faq.q: What is credential stuffing?
faq.a: Trying username and password pairs leaked from one breach against other services, exploiting password reuse.

49.seo_title: What Is a Password Attack? Types Explained for Beginners
49.seo_description: Learn password attack types: brute force, dictionary, rainbow table and credential stuffing, online vs offline attacks, hashing and why wordlists matter.

50.about: Chapter 50 explains hashing before any cracking tool appears. It defines a hash, distinguishes hashing from encryption, compares MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and bcrypt, explains why passwords are stored as hashes, what makes a hash one-way, how rainbow tables and brute force attempt to match hashes, and how salting changes the economics of cracking.
learn: What a hash function is and how hashing works
The difference between hashing and encryption
MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and bcrypt at a high level
Why systems store password hashes instead of plaintext
Why a hash is one-way and why that matters
How rainbow tables and brute force work against hashes
How salting strengthens password storage

concepts.p: Encryption is reversible with a key. Hashing is a one-way transformation that produces a fixed-length digest. A login system hashes the submitted password and compares digests, so it never needs to store the original.

A salt is a unique random value added before hashing, so identical passwords produce different digests and precomputed rainbow tables stop working. Password-specific algorithms such as bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 also make each guess intentionally expensive.

practical.intro: These reference commands show the difference between fast general-purpose hashes; they are not password storage recommendations.

commands.d: Compute a SHA-256 digest of a string.
Compute an MD5 digest (obsolete for security).
Hash a file to verify integrity.

practical.safety: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes. Use bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 for password storage, and never build your own authentication scheme.

faq.q: Can a hash be reversed?
faq.a: Not by design. Attackers instead guess candidate passwords, hash them and compare. Weak passwords can be recovered this way quickly.

faq.q: Why is MD5 unsuitable for passwords?
faq.a: It is fast and collision-prone, which makes large-scale guessing cheap. Password hashing should be deliberately slow and salted.

50.seo_title: What Is Hashing? Explained for Beginners (MD5 vs SHA-256)
50.seo_description: Hashing explained: how hashes differ from encryption, MD5 vs SHA-1 vs SHA-256 vs bcrypt, why passwords are hashed, rainbow tables, brute force and salting.

51.about: Chapter 51 begins the hands-on cracking workflow with Hash-Identifier. It explains why identifying the hash type is the essential first step, runs the tool against sample hashes, interprets the candidate types it returns, discusses look-alike formats, and links the result to the cracking tool and mode you choose next.
learn: Why hash identification comes before cracking
How Hash-Identifier compares a hash against known formats
How to run the tool on a sample hash
How to interpret candidate types and confidence
Why similar-looking hashes cause misidentification
How hash type determines the cracking tool and options

concepts.p: Hash length and character set narrow the possibilities, but several algorithms produce similar-looking values. Context such as the source system, a prefix like $2y$ or $6$, and the application's documentation are stronger evidence than length alone.

concepts.h: A guess is not a verification
concepts.p: Hash-Identifier returns possibilities. The reliable test is to crack a candidate or verify a known plaintext. Choosing the wrong format wastes time and can produce confusing failures.

practical.intro: The tool is interactive. Work with hashes you generated yourself in the lab.

commands.d: Start the interactive identifier and paste a lab hash.
Alternative identifier available in Kali, if installed.

practical.safety: Only analyse hashes from systems you own or are authorized to assess. A hash can contain sensitive information about the source system.

faq.q: Can Hash-Identifier crack a password?
faq.a: No. It only suggests which algorithm produced the hash. Cracking requires a separate tool and wordlist.

faq.q: What if the tool lists several possible types?
faq.a: Use context and test candidates. Formats with distinctive prefixes, such as bcrypt's $2y$, are easier to confirm.

51.seo_title: Hash-Identifier Tutorial: Identify Any Hash Type
51.seo_description: Use Hash-Identifier to identify MD5, SHA and bcrypt hashes: why format matters, how to read candidate results, and how the type selects your cracking method.

52.about: Chapter 52 is the practical bridge between theory and tools. It walks through the complete password cracking workflow, cracks a hashed password with a wordlist, contrasts online login attacks with offline hash attacks, shows how to read tool output, explains why wordlist quality and hash type determine success, and troubleshoots failures.
learn: The end-to-end password and hash cracking workflow
How to crack a lab hash with a wordlist
The practical difference between online and offline attacks
How to read cracking tool output and find recovered passwords
Why wordlist quality and hash type control success
Why a hash may fail to crack and how to troubleshoot

concepts.p: Obtain a hash, identify its format, choose a tool and wordlist, run the attack, then verify and record the result. Each stage is a source of failure, so changing one variable at a time makes troubleshooting tractable.
A wordlist attack succeeds only if the password is in the list or can be derived by a rule. Large wordlists cost time and storage, and slow hashes make GPU time the limiting factor.

practical.intro: Use a hash you created in the lab. The exact tool and options are demonstrated in the video.

commands.d: Run a wordlist attack with John the Ripper.
Display recovered passwords for the hash file.

practical.safety: Cracking hashes from real systems without authorization is illegal. Use lab-generated hashes and keep wordlists out of public repositories when they contain sensitive data.

faq.q: Why did my hash not crack?
faq.a: The password may not be in the wordlist, the hash type may be wrong, or the file format may not match what the tool expects.

faq.q: Does a bigger wordlist always help?
faq.a: It increases coverage but also runtime. Targeted lists and rules often outperform a huge generic list.

52.seo_title: Password and Hash Cracking Tutorial: Full Workflow
52.seo_description: Follow the complete password cracking workflow: choose a wordlist, crack a lab hash, read output, verify the result and troubleshoot failed attempts.

53.about: Chapter 53 turns wordlists into a targeted tool with CEWL. It explains why custom lists beat generic ones, how CEWL crawls a website to collect words, basic syntax, minimum word length and crawl depth, metadata collection for author and email terms, saving output, and combining the result with John the Ripper or Hydra.
learn: Why target-specific wordlists can outperform generic lists
How CEWL crawls a website and extracts words
Basic CEWL syntax and key options
How to control word length and crawl depth
How to include metadata such as author and email terms
How to save and reuse the generated list

concepts.p: People build passwords from company names, products, local terms and personal details. A wordlist scraped from an organization's public site captures that vocabulary, which is why it can outperform a generic breach list for a specific target.
CEWL reads publicly accessible pages. It does not attack the site, but crawling still generates requests and should stay within scope and reasonable rate limits.

practical.intro: Crawl a site you own or are authorized to assess, and save the output outside the repository.

commands.d: Crawl two levels deep, keep words of five or more characters, save to a file.
Include email addresses found on the site.
Check how many candidates the crawl produced.

practical.safety: Do not publish wordlists containing personal data. Crawling can be logged and rate-limited; use a modest depth and respect robots and scope.

faq.q: What does the -m option do in CEWL?
faq.a: It sets the minimum word length, filtering out short noise that is unlikely to be useful.

faq.q: Can CEWL replace rockyou.txt?
faq.a: No. It produces a targeted supplement. Combining a targeted list with a broad list often works best.

53.seo_title: CEWL Tutorial: Build Custom Wordlists from Websites
53.seo_description: Build targeted wordlists with CEWL: crawl a site, set depth and minimum length, collect metadata, save the list and use it with John or Hydra.

54.about: Chapter 54 introduces Crunch, the pattern-based wordlist generator. It contrasts Crunch with CEWL's scraping approach, shows how to set minimum and maximum length, define character sets, use patterns based on partial knowledge, save output, estimate list size and storage, and decide between Crunch, CEWL and pre-built lists.
learn: What Crunch is and how it differs from CEWL
How to set minimum and maximum password length
How to define custom character sets
How to use patterns for partially known passwords
How to save generated lists and estimate their size
When to use Crunch, CEWL or a pre-built wordlist

concepts.p: Each added character position multiplies the search space. An eight-character lowercase-only space is 26^8; adding digits and symbols increases it enormously. Always calculate the size before generating, or you may fill the disk.

If you know a password starts with a company name and ends with four digits, a Crunch pattern encodes that assumption and avoids generating irrelevant combinations. That is far more efficient than blind brute force.

practical.intro: Generate small lists first so you can inspect them. The syntax is length min, length max, character set.

commands.d: Generate all four-digit numeric combinations.
Generate six- to eight-character combinations and save to a file.
Use a pattern where @ stands for lowercase letters.
Check the size of the generated wordlist.

practical.safety: Large character sets can exhaust disk space and take hours. Set a small range, test the count first, and store generated lists outside the repository.

faq.q: How do I estimate a Crunch wordlist size?
faq.a: Raise the character-set size to the length for fixed-length output, then sum across lengths. Crunch prints the number of lines before generating.

faq.q: What does the @ symbol mean in a Crunch pattern?
faq.a: It represents a lowercase letter placeholder. Other symbols represent uppercase letters, digits and symbols as documented by the tool.

54.seo_title: Crunch Tutorial: Generate Wordlists with Custom Patterns
54.seo_description: Generate wordlists with Crunch: length ranges, custom character sets, pattern-based generation, size estimation and when to use it instead of CEWL.

55.about: Chapter 55 puts the password section together with John the Ripper. It explains why John is a standard offline cracking tool, contrasts offline and online attacks, demonstrates basic syntax and wordlist usage, explains single, wordlist and incremental modes, shows --show for recovered passwords, and cracks a password-protected file format as well as a hash.
learn: What John the Ripper is and why it is used offline
Why offline cracking is usually faster than online guessing
Basic John syntax and wordlist attacks
The difference between single, wordlist and incremental modes
How to display recovered passwords with --show
How to extract and crack password-protected file hashes

concepts.p: Single mode derives candidates from account information, wordlist mode tries a supplied list with optional rules, and incremental mode explores a character space. Choosing a mode is choosing which guesses you believe are most likely.

concepts.h: Cracking files uses the same pipeline
concepts.p: Tools such as zip2john extract a verifiable hash from a protected archive. John then attacks that hash. The archive itself is not decrypted by brute force; the password is recovered, then used normally.

practical.intro: Use hashes and archives you created in the lab. Install the jumbo package if a format is not recognised.

commands.d: Run a wordlist attack against a lab hash file.
Run an incremental brute-force attack (slow).
Print recovered passwords.
Extract a verifiable hash from a ZIP archive.
Crack the extracted archive hash.

practical.safety: Only crack hashes and files you own or are authorized to assess. Recovering a password does not grant permission to access the underlying data.

faq.q: Why does John not recognise my hash?
faq.a: The format may need an explicit --format option, or the file may contain extra text. Use the matching *2john tool where possible.

faq.q: What is the fastest John mode?
faq.a: It depends on the target. Wordlist mode with good rules is often fastest for human-chosen passwords; incremental mode is exhaustive and slow.

55.seo_title: Crack Passwords Offline with John the Ripper
55.seo_description: Learn John the Ripper: wordlist, single and incremental modes, --show, and cracking ZIP archive hashes with zip2john in an isolated lab.

56.about: Chapter 56 applies cracking skills to operating system credential stores. It explains where Windows keeps hashes in the SAM file and Linux in /etc/shadow, how each is structured, how to extract hashes with proper authorization, how unshadow combines passwd and shadow for John, and how the formats differ.

Where Linux stores password hashes in /etc/shadow
How to extract hashes with proper authorization
How to combine /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow with unshadow
How to crack the combined file with John the Ripper
How Windows and Linux hash formats differ

concepts.h: Shadow files exist for a reason
concepts.p: Historically, password hashes lived in /etc/passwd, which every user can read. Modern systems move them to /etc/shadow, readable only by root. That change makes offline cracking require privileged access first.

The SAM database stores local account password material and is locked while Windows runs. Authorized forensic acquisition uses supported methods and produces hash formats that cracking tools understand, such as NTLM.

practical.intro: Demonstrations require a lab VM you own and administrative access. Commands below use a copy of the files, not the live originals.

commands.d: Copy the files in an authorized lab for offline review.
Merge passwd and shadow into a John-compatible file.
Crack the combined lab hashes.
Show recovered lab passwords.

practical.safety: Extracting credential stores from systems you do not own is illegal and harmful. Never copy real user hashes into a repository, chat or shared storage.

faq.q: Why can a normal user read /etc/passwd but not /etc/shadow?
faq.a: /etc/passwd contains account information and is world-readable. /etc/shadow contains password hashes and is restricted to root.

faq.q: What is unshadow used for?
faq.a: It combines the account data in passwd with the hashes in shadow so John the Ripper can associate each hash with a username.

56.seo_title: Extract and Crack SAM and Shadow Hashes (Lab)
56.seo_description: Understand Windows SAM and Linux /etc/shadow, extract hashes with authorization, combine passwd and shadow with unshadow, and crack lab credentials with John.

57.about: Chapter 57 applies the extract-then-crack workflow to archives and documents. It explains why protected files need a different approach, extracts hashes from ZIP and RAR files with zip2john and rar2john, cracks them with John and a wordlist, extends the method to PDFs with pdf2john, and discusses choosing a context-aware wordlist.
learn: Why password-protected files require hash extraction first
How to extract a ZIP hash with zip2john
How to extract a RAR hash with rar2john
How to crack the hash with John and a wordlist
How the same approach applies to PDFs and other formats
How file context guides wordlist selection

concepts.p: Archive formats store enough information to test a candidate password without decrypting the whole file. The *2john helpers convert that information into a hash line John can attack efficiently.

A file from a named project, client or year gives clues for a targeted wordlist or rule set. Blind brute force against modern encryption is rarely practical; context and wordlist quality decide the outcome.

practical.intro: Create your own password-protected test archives. The helpers ship with John the Ripper jumbo.

commands.d: Extract a verifiable hash from a ZIP file.
Extract a hash from a RAR file.
Extract a hash from a PDF.
Crack the extracted hash with a wordlist.

practical.safety: Crack only files you created or are authorized to recover. Many archives contain personal or business data, and unauthorized access is illegal.

faq.q: Can John open the archive directly?
faq.a: Not usually. You extract a hash with the matching *2john helper, crack the password, then use the password with the normal extraction tool.

faq.q: Does this work on every encrypted file?
faq.a: Only formats with a supported extraction helper. Strong encryption and long random passwords can make recovery impractical.

57.seo_title: Crack RAR and ZIP File Passwords with John the Ripper
57.seo_description: Recover archive passwords in a lab: extract hashes with zip2john, rar2john and pdf2john, crack them with John and a wordlist, and choose better wordlists.

58.about: Chapter 58 switches from offline cracking to online guessing with THC Hydra. It recaps the online versus offline distinction, explains which services Hydra supports, covers basic syntax, demonstrates SSH and web form attacks, shows how to use wordlists, how to read successful-login output, and why lockouts and rate limits change the economics.
learn: How online attacks differ from offline cracking
Which services and protocols Hydra can test
Basic Hydra syntax and command structure
How to test an SSH login in a lab
How to test a web login form in a lab
How lockouts, rate limits and logging affect online attacks

concepts.p: An online attack sends authentication requests to a live service. That creates logs, triggers alerts and is constrained by lockout policies. Hydra's speed cannot overcome a server that stops answering after five failures.

concepts.h: Form attacks depend on request shape
concepts.p: Web login modules need the correct form path, field names and failure string. A single mismatch produces false negatives, so capture a real request from your lab app and verify one known-good credential first.

practical.intro: Use only lab services you own. Hydra syntax follows the service module, target, user and password list.

commands.d: Test SSH credentials against a lab host.
Test FTP credentials with user and password lists.
Test a lab web form; field names and failure text must match your app.

practical.safety: Online brute force against systems you do not own is illegal and can lock out real users. Respect rate limits, stop after the agreed scope, and never test production accounts.

faq.q: Why is Hydra slower than offline cracking?
faq.a: Each guess requires a network request and a server response, and defences such as lockouts or delays limit attempts.

faq.q: Why does my web form attack report zero results?
faq.a: The form path, parameter names or failure indicator is probably wrong. Verify with a browser request and a known credential first.

58.seo_title: THC Hydra Tutorial: Online Password Attacks for Beginners
58.seo_description: Learn THC Hydra: online vs offline attacks, SSH and web form syntax, wordlists, reading results, and why lockouts make online guessing different.

59.about: Chapter 59 introduces Medusa as a parallel alternative to Hydra. It compares the two tools, explains Medusa's syntax, demonstrates SSH and other service modules, shows how to supply username and password lists, discusses its parallel testing model, and helps you choose between Medusa and Hydra for a given service.
learn: What Medusa is and how it compares with Hydra
Basic Medusa syntax and module structure
How to test SSH credentials in a lab
How to target other supported services such as FTP and Telnet
How parallel testing affects speed and reliability
When to choose Medusa or Hydra

concepts.p: Medusa can test multiple hosts and credentials concurrently. That improves throughput against tolerant services but increases the chance of lockouts, dropped connections and inaccurate results on fragile targets.
Each service has a module that knows the protocol's login exchange. Using the wrong module or port produces failures that look like wrong passwords, so verify the service and port first.

practical.intro: Run against lab services only. Replace host, module and lists with your own values.

commands.d: Test SSH with a single username.
Test FTP with user and password lists.
Limit parallel tasks to reduce load and lockouts.

practical.safety: Keep concurrency low and stop on success. Online guessing can lock accounts and disrupt services; only test systems you own or are authorized to assess.

faq.q: Is Medusa faster than Hydra?
faq.a: It can be, because of its parallel model, but real speed depends on the service, network latency and defensive controls.

faq.q: What does the -M option do?
faq.a: It selects the service module Medusa uses to speak the target protocol.

59.seo_title: Medusa Tutorial: Online Password Brute Forcing
59.seo_description: Use Medusa for online password testing: syntax, SSH and FTP modules, parallel testing trade-offs, and how it compares with THC Hydra.

60.about: Chapter 60 opens the network attack section by distinguishing two related techniques. It defines sniffing as capturing traffic and spoofing as impersonating an identity, compares passive and active sniffing, lists ARP, IP, MAC and DNS spoofing, explains why unencrypted traffic is vulnerable, and previews Wireshark and Ettercap.
learn: What network sniffing is and what it captures
What spoofing is and how it fakes identity on a network
The difference between sniffing and spoofing
Passive versus active sniffing
Common spoofing types: ARP, IP, MAC and DNS
Why encryption changes the impact of sniffing

concepts.p: Sniffing observes packets; spoofing changes how a device or identity appears so traffic is sent somewhere else. They are often combined: spoofing redirects traffic, then sniffing captures it.

Modern switched networks do not broadcast every frame to every port, which limits passive capture. Techniques such as ARP spoofing or port mirroring are needed to see other devices' traffic, and both require authorization.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and prepares the Wireshark and Ettercap labs that follow.
practical.safety: Intercepting other people's traffic is illegal without authorization, even on a network you can access. Use isolated lab networks for practice.

faq.q: Can I sniff traffic on a switched network?
faq.a: Not all of it by default. You see broadcast traffic and your own unicast traffic unless you use an authorized technique such as port mirroring or ARP spoofing.

faq.q: Does HTTPS stop sniffing?
faq.a: It stops content from being read in plaintext, but metadata such as destination addresses and timing may still be visible.

60.seo_title: What Is Sniffing and Spoofing in Ethical Hacking?
60.seo_description: Sniffing and spoofing explained: passive vs active capture, ARP, IP, MAC and DNS spoofing, why unencrypted traffic is vulnerable, and the tools used next.

61.about: Chapter 61 turns the sniffing concept into a practical Wireshark skill. It explains why Wireshark is the standard protocol analyser, how to choose an interface and start a capture, how the packet list, details and bytes panes relate, how display filters isolate traffic, how to follow a TCP stream, and how to recognise unencrypted data and save captures.
