How to select an interface and start a capture
How to navigate the packet list, details and bytes panes
How to write display filters by address, protocol and port
How to follow a TCP stream
How to identify plaintext data and export captures

concepts.p: Wireshark shows individual frames but can reconstruct a higher-level conversation. Following a TCP stream joins the packets of one connection so you can read the application exchange rather than inspecting it packet by packet.

concepts.h: Display filters are applied after capture
concepts.p: Display filters such as ip.addr == 192.168.56.101 or http hide packets without discarding them. Capture filters decide what is recorded in the first place, which is the subject of the next chapter.

practical.intro: Capture on your own lab interface. Filter examples assume a lab subnet; adjust addresses to match.

commands.d: Launch Wireshark with capture permissions.
Display filter for traffic to or from one host.
Display filter for HTTP traffic.
Display filter for TCP port 80.
Reassemble a TCP conversation from the packet context menu.

practical.safety: Capturing other users' traffic without authorization is illegal. Use a host-only lab network, and treat capture files as sensitive because they may contain credentials.

faq.q: Why can't Wireshark see other devices' traffic?
faq.a: On a switched network, unicast frames are delivered only to the destination port. You need your own traffic, a mirrored port or an authorized redirection technique.

faq.q: What is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter?
faq.a: A capture filter decides what is recorded. A display filter hides packets from the recorded set without deleting them.

61.seo_title: How to Use Wireshark for Network Sniffing
61.seo_description: Wireshark for beginners: choose an interface, capture traffic, navigate packet panes, use display filters, follow TCP streams and save evidence.

62.about: Chapter 62 goes deeper into capturing packets efficiently. It contrasts capture filters with display filters, covers wired and wireless interfaces, shows how to reduce noise before capture starts, demonstrates HTTP and login traffic capture, explains stopping, saving and reopening .pcap files, and offers practical tips for manageable captures.
learn: Capture filters versus display filters
How to capture on wired and wireless interfaces
How to use capture filters to reduce noise
How to capture HTTP traffic and spot plaintext data
How to observe a login exchange on an unencrypted lab service
How to save, reopen and share .pcap files

concepts.p: A busy interface can produce gigabytes quickly. Capture filters such as host 192.168.56.101 and port 80 reduce the data at the source, which keeps files small and analysis focused. The trade-off is that excluded traffic is gone permanently.

HTTP requests, form posts and many legacy protocols are readable in a capture. Seeing a username and password in cleartext is a powerful demonstration of why TLS matters, and a reminder to treat packet captures as sensitive evidence.

practical.intro: Start with a narrow capture filter, reproduce one action in your lab, then stop and save.

commands.d: Capture filter limited to one host.
Capture filter for HTTP traffic.
Save the capture as a .pcap or .pcapng file.
Read a saved capture from the command line if tshark is installed.

practical.safety: Packet captures can contain passwords, tokens and personal data. Store them securely, do not commit them to Git, and delete them when the engagement ends.

faq.q: Which filter should I use first?
faq.a: Start with a capture filter for the specific host and port you need. It keeps the file small and analysis focused.

faq.q: Can I capture Wi-Fi traffic?
faq.a: Only traffic your adapter can see. Capturing other wireless clients usually requires monitor mode and, for encrypted networks, additional material such as the handshake.

62.seo_title: Capture Network Packets with Wireshark: Practical Guide
62.seo_description: Capture packets efficiently with Wireshark: capture vs display filters, wired and wireless interfaces, HTTP traffic, login analysis, and saving pcap files.

63.about: Chapter 63 explains why Wireshark cannot see another machine's traffic by default and the legitimate ways to capture it. It covers switched-network behaviour, SPAN and port mirroring, ARP spoofing as a man-in-the-middle technique, tools such as arpspoof and Ettercap, remote capture over SSH with tcpdump, and gateway capture. Authorization is a recurring theme.
learn: Why switched networks limit what Wireshark can see
How port mirroring and SPAN ports provide authorized remote capture
How ARP spoofing redirects traffic for interception
How arpspoof and Ettercap support man-in-the-middle capture
How to pipe remote capture over SSH with tcpdump
Why capture on a gateway or router sees more traffic
What authorized access actually requires

concepts.p: A managed switch can copy traffic from one port to another. This is the standard, authorized way for administrators to feed an analyser. It requires control of the switch and does not alter traffic.

ARP spoofing poisons a host's cache so it sends traffic through the attacker's machine. It can disrupt connectivity, is detectable, and is illegal without authorization. In a lab it is a controlled demonstration of why dynamic ARP inspection and encryption matter.

practical.intro: In an isolated lab you own, capture remote traffic through a mirrored port or an SSH tunnel. The commands below are examples; adapt interfaces and addresses.

commands.d: Stream a remote capture over SSH into Wireshark.
Lab-only ARP redirection; requires authorization and clean-up.
Enable forwarding so the lab target keeps connectivity during the demonstration.

practical.safety: ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle capture on networks you do not own is illegal and disruptive. Use a host-only lab, tell any affected users, and restore ARP tables and forwarding settings afterwards.

faq.q: What is a SPAN port?
faq.a: A switched port analyser configuration that copies traffic from selected ports or VLANs to a monitoring port.

faq.q: Does remote capture require root on the remote host?
faq.a: Packet capture usually requires elevated privileges. Use an account and method approved by the system owner.

63.seo_title: Remote Packet Capture: How Wireshark Sees Other Machines
63.seo_description: How analysts capture traffic from another machine: SPAN ports, ARP spoofing and MITM concepts, SSH remote capture with tcpdump, and legal authorization.

64.about: Chapter 64 builds the conceptual foundation for the spoofing labs. It defines spoofing as impersonating a trusted identity, then explains ARP cache poisoning, IP source forgery, DNS spoofing and cache poisoning, MAC spoofing and the idea of spoofing beyond the network layer. It closes with defences and legal boundaries.
learn: What spoofing means at the network and identity level
How ARP spoofing poisons local caches and redirects LAN traffic
How IP spoofing forges source addresses
How DNS spoofing and cache poisoning redirect name resolution
How MAC spoofing changes a device's link-layer identity
How dynamic ARP inspection, DNSSEC and filtering defend against spoofing

concepts.p: ARP has no authentication: a host accepts a reply claiming an address belongs to a MAC. DNS without DNSSEC also trusts responses. Spoofing exploits that missing verification, which is why the defences focus on validating the claim.

Dynamic ARP inspection, DHCP snooping, static ARP entries, DNSSEC, encrypted protocols and network segmentation each raise the cost of spoofing. No single control eliminates it, especially on hostile local networks.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual and prepares the Ettercap and DNS spoofing demonstrations.
practical.safety: Spoofing attacks disrupt other users and are illegal without written authorization. Practise only on isolated lab equipment you own.

faq.q: How is ARP spoofing different from IP spoofing?
faq.a: ARP spoofing manipulates local address resolution so traffic flows through the attacker. IP spoofing forges the source address in packet headers and usually prevents return traffic from reaching the sender.

faq.q: Does HTTPS prevent DNS spoofing?
faq.a: HTTPS certificate validation makes it hard to impersonate a site even if DNS is poisoned, which is why certificate warnings must never be ignored.

64.seo_title: Spoofing Attacks Explained: ARP, DNS and IP Spoofing
64.seo_description: Learn how spoofing works: ARP cache poisoning, IP source forgery, DNS spoofing and MAC spoofing, plus the defences that detect or prevent each attack.

65.about: Chapter 65 demonstrates DNS spoofing in an isolated lab. It reviews normal DNS resolution, explains how spoofed responses redirect a victim, sets up a spoofing demonstration with Ettercap or dnsspoof, combines DNS spoofing with ARP spoofing for a full man-in-the-middle path, and discusses real-world impact and defences.
learn: How normal DNS resolution works
What DNS spoofing and cache poisoning change
How a victim is redirected to a fake site
How to build a DNS spoofing demonstration in a lab
How DNS and ARP spoofing combine into a man-in-the-middle chain
How DNSSEC, static entries and detection reduce risk

concepts.p: DNS spoofing works by supplying a forged answer before or instead of the legitimate one, or by poisoning a resolver's cache. The victim then connects to the address the attacker chose while the domain name looks correct.

Redirecting DNS does not automatically defeat TLS. A fake site without a valid certificate triggers a browser warning. Users who click through warnings, or sites that serve mixed or unencrypted content, remain exposed.

practical.intro: The lab uses ettercap or dnsspoof on an isolated network with machines you own. The video shows the exact configuration.

commands.d: Lab-only ARP MITM session to position traffic for DNS manipulation.
Serve spoofed DNS answers from a mapping file in the lab.
Review the spoofed name-to-address mappings used in the demo.

practical.safety: DNS spoofing can steal credentials and is illegal outside an authorized test. Use an isolated lab, avoid real credentials, and restore network settings afterwards.

faq.q: What is the difference between DNS spoofing and DNS cache poisoning?
faq.a: Spoofing supplies a forged response to a query. Cache poisoning inserts a forged record into a resolver's cache so many users receive it.

faq.q: How do I defend against DNS spoofing?
faq.a: Use DNSSEC where available, encrypted DNS, trusted resolvers, static entries for critical hosts, and network controls that prevent ARP manipulation.

65.seo_title: DNS Spoofing Attack Explained and Demonstrated
65.seo_description: DNS spoofing explained: how forged answers redirect victims, a lab demonstration with Ettercap and dnsspoof, combined ARP MITM, impact and defences.

66.about: Chapter 66 is a setup chapter for Ettercap. It explains what Ettercap does in a penetration test, compares graphical and console modes, sets the correct interface, edits etter.conf for privilege and iptables settings, enables the DNS spoof plugin, configures etter.dns, chooses unified or bridged sniffing, and fixes common configuration errors.
learn: What Ettercap is and where it fits in a test
When to use the GUI versus console mode
How to select the correct network interface
How to review etter.conf and its privilege settings
How to enable and configure the DNS spoof plugin
How to troubleshoot interface, permission and plugin errors

concepts.p: Ettercap's core handles capture and man-in-the-middle positioning; plugins add behaviour such as DNS spoofing. The etter.dns file maps names to addresses, and the plugin must be activated in the running session.

Raw capture requires elevated privileges, and the tool must listen on the interface that carries the target traffic. Most setup failures are a wrong interface, an unreadable configuration or a plugin that was never loaded.

practical.intro: Configure Ettercap on your own lab VM. Read the configuration before changing privilege settings.

commands.d: Start the graphical interface.
Start console mode on a chosen interface.
Review privilege and iptables settings.
Review DNS spoof mappings before enabling the plugin.

practical.safety: Running Ettercap on a shared network disrupts users and may be illegal. Keep the lab isolated, announce the test to any participants, and restore configuration afterwards.

faq.q: Where is etter.conf on Kali Linux?
faq.a: Current packages place it under /etc/ettercap/. Older guides reference /etc/etter.conf, so check the path on your installed version.

faq.q: Why does the DNS spoof plugin not appear?
faq.a: The plugin may not be loaded, the configuration file may be missing or unreadable, or the interface may be wrong. Check the startup log for the first error.

66.seo_title: How to Configure Ettercap on Kali Linux (Step by Step)
66.seo_description: Configure Ettercap for lab work: GUI vs console mode, interface selection, etter.conf settings, DNS spoof plugin, etter.dns and common errors.

67.about: Chapter 67 opens the wireless section with terminology rather than tools. It defines SSID and BSSID, access points and stations, channels and frequency bands, WEP through WPA3, the four-way handshake, monitor versus managed mode, packet injection, deauthentication frames, PMKID, and basic wireless defences.
learn: The difference between SSID and BSSID
Access points versus client stations
How channels and the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands differ
What changed from WEP to WPA, WPA2 and WPA3
What the four-way handshake is and why capturing it matters
Why monitor mode and packet injection depend on adapter support
What PMKID, hidden networks and MAC filtering do

concepts.p: Unlike a switched wired network, radio frames are broadcast through the air. Encryption protects content, but management frames and metadata are still visible to nearby adapters. That is why wireless assessment starts with understanding frames and encryption.

WPA2 cracking usually requires a captured four-way handshake or PMKID, then an offline dictionary attack against it. A strong, unique passphrase makes that attack impractical. WEP is different: its design flaws allow key recovery from collected traffic.

practical.intro: This chapter is conceptual. The following chapters apply these terms with Aircrack-ng and Fern.
practical.safety: Wireless attacks affect nearby networks and users. Test only your own access point in an isolated lab, and never deauthenticate or capture traffic on networks you do not own.

faq.q: What is the difference between SSID and BSSID?
faq.a: The SSID is the network name users see. The BSSID is the MAC address of a specific access point radio.

faq.q: Is WEP still used?
faq.a: Rarely, and it should not be. WEP is fundamentally broken and can be cracked quickly regardless of password strength.

67.seo_title: WiFi Hacking Basics: Terms You Must Know First
67.seo_description: Wireless security terms explained: SSID vs BSSID, access points, channels, WEP to WPA3, the four-way handshake, monitor mode, injection and PMKID.

68.about: Chapter 68 demonstrates the classic WEP attack with Aircrack-ng in a lab. It reviews why WEP is broken, puts the adapter into monitor mode with airmon-ng, scans for WEP networks with airodump-ng, collects IVs, uses fake authentication and injection with aireplay-ng, cracks the key, and verifies it. The demo uses the presenter's own router.
learn: Why WEP is fundamentally insecure
How to enable monitor mode with airmon-ng
How to scan for networks with airodump-ng
How IV collection and packet injection accelerate a WEP attack
How to crack a WEP key with aircrack-ng
Why WEP was deprecated and replaced

concepts.h: A design flaw, not a weak password
concepts.p: WEP's small IV space and weak integrity checks allow an attacker to recover the key from enough captured traffic. Changing the WEP password to something long does not fix the underlying protocol.

Monitor mode lets the adapter capture all frames on a channel, not just those addressed to it. Injection lets the tester send crafted frames, which speeds up IV collection. Both require hardware and drivers that support them.

practical.intro: The demonstration uses the presenter's own WEP-configured router in an isolated lab. Replace interface and BSSID values with your lab equipment.

commands.d: Enable monitor mode on the wireless adapter.
Scan nearby networks and note the target BSSID and channel.
Capture traffic from the target network.
Associate with the lab access point.
Attempt to recover the WEP key from the capture.

practical.safety: Never attack a neighbour's or public network. Wireless injection can disrupt legitimate traffic, and unauthorized interception is illegal.

faq.q: Why is WEP so easy to crack?
faq.a: Its initialization vectors are too short and reused, and its integrity check is weak, so enough traffic reveals the key.

faq.q: Does my adapter support monitor mode?
faq.a: It depends on the chipset and driver. Internal laptop cards often do not; adapters with supported Atheros or Realtek chipsets are commonly used.

68.seo_title: Crack WEP WiFi with Aircrack-ng (Step-by-Step Lab)
68.seo_description: Learn the WEP attack workflow in a lab: monitor mode with airmon-ng, capture with airodump-ng, injection with aireplay-ng, and cracking with aircrack-ng.

69.about: Chapter 69 moves to WPA/WPA2, the far more common wireless security standard. It explains why the attack is different, demonstrates monitor mode and target scanning, captures the four-way handshake, uses a deauthentication frame to speed it up, verifies the capture, and runs an offline wordlist attack with aircrack-ng. Wordlist quality is central.
learn: Why WPA/WPA2 resists the WEP approach
How to scan targets with airodump-ng
How to capture a four-way handshake
How a deauthentication attack forces a reconnect
How to verify a valid handshake capture
How to run an offline wordlist attack with aircrack-ng
Why passphrase strength determines the outcome

concepts.p: The four-way handshake proves both sides know the pre-shared key without transmitting it. An attacker can capture the exchange and test candidate passphrases offline by deriving the same keys.

concepts.h: Dictionary attacks depend on the passphrase
concepts.p: Aircrack-ng tries each wordlist entry against the captured handshake. If the passphrase is long, random and absent from the list, the attack fails. This is why a unique passphrase of sufficient length is an effective defence.

practical.intro: Use your own access point with a weak test passphrase. Replace interface, channel and BSSID values.

commands.d: Put the adapter into monitor mode.
Capture traffic from the target channel.
Send deauthentication frames in the lab to force a reconnect.
Run the offline wordlist attack against the captured handshake.

practical.safety: Deauthentication disconnects users and can disrupt critical services. Use it only on your own lab access point, for a few frames, and never on public or neighbour networks.

faq.q: Can WPA2 be cracked without a handshake?
faq.a: A dictionary attack needs a handshake or PMKID to test candidates. Without that material there is nothing to verify guesses against.

faq.q: Does a long password make WPA2 safe?
faq.a: A long, random, unique passphrase makes offline guessing impractical, which is the main practical defence. WPA3 improves the protocol further.

69.seo_title: Crack WPA/WPA2 WiFi Passwords with Aircrack-ng
69.seo_description: WPA2 handshake capture and offline cracking in a lab: airodump-ng, deauth, verifying the handshake, aircrack-ng with a wordlist and passphrase defence.

70.about: Chapter 70 repeats the wireless workflow through a GUI. It explains that Fern WiFi Cracker automates Aircrack-ng components, shows how to select an interface, switch to monitor mode inside the app, scan networks, run automated WEP and wordlist-based WPA/WPA2 attacks, use session management, and compares the GUI with the manual command-line process.
learn: What Fern WiFi Cracker is and how it relates to Aircrack-ng
How to select the correct wireless interface
How to enable monitor mode from the GUI
How to scan for WEP and WPA/WPA2 networks
How to run automated WEP and WPA/WPA2 tests
How the GUI compares with the manual workflow

concepts.h: A front end, not a different attack
concepts.p: Fern orchestrates the same underlying tools and techniques. Learning the command-line process first makes the GUI understandable and helps when a step fails silently.

GUI tools choose interfaces, channels and attack steps for you. That convenience can obscure what is happening and make it easier to act outside your authorization. Verify the target and scope before starting any automated attack.

practical.intro: Run Fern in a lab VM with a supported adapter and your own access point.

commands.d: Launch Fern from a terminal if it is not in the application menu.

practical.safety: Automated wireless attacks can disrupt many users at once. Use only your own lab network, and never leave an attack running unattended.

faq.q: Is Fern better than Aircrack-ng?
faq.a: It is easier for beginners because it automates steps. The command line gives more control and better diagnostics.

faq.q: Why does Fern not detect my adapter?
faq.a: The driver may not support monitor mode or injection, or the interface may be in use. Check adapter compatibility first.

70.seo_title: Fern WiFi Cracker Tutorial: GUI WEP/WPA2 Testing
70.seo_description: Use Fern WiFi Cracker in a lab: interface selection, monitor mode, network scanning, automated WEP and WPA/WPA2 tests, and GUI vs Aircrack-ng trade-offs.

71.about: Chapter 71 opens the exploitation section with the Metasploit Framework. It explains why Metasploit is central to professional testing, describes exploits, payloads, auxiliary and post modules, tours msfconsole, explains the exploit-payload relationship, and demonstrates search, show options, set and set payload. Metasploitable is introduced as a safe practice target.
learn: What Metasploit is and where it fits in a penetration test
The core module types: exploits, payloads, auxiliary and post
How to launch and navigate msfconsole
How the exploit and payload relationship works
How to search for modules and inspect their options
How to set parameters and payloads for a module

concepts.p: An exploit delivers code by abusing a vulnerability. A payload is what runs after successful delivery, such as a shell. The same exploit can often use several payloads, which is why configuration is a two-part decision.

concepts.h: A framework, not a target list
concepts.p: Metasploit organises modules and sessions but does not find targets for you. Reconnaissance and scanning identify the service and version; the framework helps you act on that information within an authorized scope.

practical.intro: Practise navigation against Metasploitable in an isolated lab. These commands change no target until you run an exploit.

commands.d: Start the Metasploit console.
Search for modules related to a service.
Load an auxiliary scanner module.
Display the module's required settings.
Set the target host for the loaded module.
Select a payload for an exploit module.

practical.safety: Metasploit is powerful and easy to misuse. Run exploits only against intentionally vulnerable lab machines you own, and never against systems without written authorization.

faq.q: What is Metasploitable?
faq.a: A deliberately vulnerable virtual machine maintained for practising exploitation in an isolated lab.

faq.q: Does Metasploit require a database?
faq.a: It works without one, but the PostgreSQL database enables workspace management and faster search of hosts, services and credentials.

71.seo_title: What Is Metasploit? Beginner's Guide to the Framework
71.seo_description: Metasploit for beginners: exploits, payloads, auxiliary and post modules, msfconsole navigation, search, show options and setting targets safely in a lab.

72.about: Chapter 72 runs a first real exploit. It explains buffer overflows conceptually, sets up an intentionally vulnerable lab target, uses Nmap to identify the service, searches Metasploit for a matching module, configures the target and payload, launches the exploit, obtains a session, and performs basic post-exploitation checks. Modern mitigations close the lesson.
learn: What a buffer overflow is at a conceptual level
Why overwriting memory can redirect program execution
How to identify a vulnerable service with Nmap
How to find and configure a matching Metasploit module
How to select a payload and launch the exploit in a lab
How to confirm access and explore a session
How ASLR, DEP and patching make exploitation harder

concepts.p: A buffer overflow writes beyond allocated memory and can overwrite control data such as a return address. If the attacker controls the overwritten value, execution can be redirected to their code.

Address space layout randomisation, data execution prevention, stack canaries, compiler hardening and prompt patching each complicate exploitation. Many real-world compromises combine a memory bug with an information leak to bypass these protections.

practical.intro: Use an intentionally vulnerable lab VM in an isolated network. The video demonstrates module selection and payload configuration.

commands.d: Identify the vulnerable service and version.
Start Metasploit.
Search for a matching exploit module.
Load the module.
Set the lab target address.
Set the reverse-shell listener address on your lab machine.
Launch the exploit against the lab target.
Interact with the first session.

practical.safety: Exploitation can crash services and is illegal without authorization. Use snapshots, isolate the lab network, and never test real systems.

faq.q: What is a reverse shell payload?
faq.a: The target connects back to the attacker's listener, which often bypasses inbound firewall rules. It requires a reachable listener address.

faq.q: Why does an exploit fail on a patched system?
faq.a: The vulnerability may be fixed, the target version may differ from the module's assumptions, or mitigations may prevent reliable exploitation.

72.seo_title: Exploit a Buffer Overflow with Metasploit (Lab Demo)
72.seo_description: Understand buffer overflows and run a Metasploit exploit in an isolated lab: Nmap service discovery, module configuration, payloads, sessions and mitigations.

73.about: Chapter 73 shifts to defence with honeypots. It defines a honeypot as a decoy system, compares low- and high-interaction designs, lists server, client, malware and network honeypots, explains why organizations deploy them, demonstrates a basic setup, covers monitoring and analysis, and discusses the legal and ethical issues of running one.
learn: What a honeypot is and how it differs from production systems
Low-interaction versus high-interaction trade-offs
Common honeypot types and their purposes
Why organizations deploy honeypots
How to monitor and analyse activity against a honeypot
The legal and ethical responsibilities of operating one

concepts.p: A honeypot has no legitimate production purpose, so any interaction is suspicious. That makes it a high-signal detection source and a way to study attacker behaviour without exposing real assets.
A compromised honeypot must not become a pivot into the real network. Isolation, logging, egress filtering and clear rules of engagement are prerequisites, not optional hardening.

practical.intro: The chapter demonstrates a basic honeypot in a lab. Keep any honeypot on an isolated segment with no route to production systems.
practical.safety: Do not deploy a honeypot on a network you do not control. Enticing or recording real users can create legal and privacy obligations, and a poorly contained honeypot is a liability.

faq.q: Is running a honeypot legal?
faq.a: Generally yes on your own network, but recording attackers and handling their data creates legal and privacy duties that vary by jurisdiction.

faq.q: What is the difference between low- and high-interaction honeypots?
faq.a: Low-interaction honeypots emulate limited services and are safer and easier to run. High-interaction honeypots provide real systems, yielding richer data but much greater risk.

73.seo_title: Honeypots Explained: How Security Teams Trap Attackers
73.seo_description: What is a honeypot? Low- vs high-interaction designs, honeypot types, why organizations deploy them, monitoring attacker activity, and legal containment.

74.about: Chapter 74 puts honeypot theory into practice with Pentbox. It introduces the toolkit, shows how to download and install it with its Ruby dependencies, navigates the menu interface, configures the built-in honeypot, tests it from another machine, reviews logged activity, and briefly explores other modules such as the port scanner and password generator.
learn: What Pentbox is and which utilities it bundles
How to install Pentbox and its Ruby dependencies
How to navigate the menu-driven interface
How to configure and start the honeypot module
How to test the honeypot and observe logged connections
Which other Pentbox modules are useful in a small lab

concepts.p: Pentbox's honeypot listens on a port and logs connections. Any connection is interesting because there is no legitimate service. Simple decoys like this are useful for learning detection and for early warning on a small network.
Pentbox is a Ruby application, so it needs a working Ruby interpreter. Installing dependencies from a package manager is safer than running arbitrary gem installs as root.

practical.intro: Install in a lab VM and expose the honeypot only to your isolated lab network. The exact menu choices are demonstrated in the video.

commands.d: Check whether Ruby is installed.
Install Ruby from the distribution repositories.
Clone the repository shown in the tutorial.
Start the menu-driven interface.

practical.safety: Keep the honeypot off any network with production systems and do not publish its address. Logs may contain personal data, so retain them responsibly.

faq.q: Is Pentbox still maintained?
faq.a: It is an older tool. It remains useful for learning, but check compatibility and prefer maintained alternatives for production monitoring.

faq.q: Can a honeypot stop an attacker?
faq.a: No. It detects and observes. Blocking and containment come from firewalls, segmentation and monitoring systems.

74.seo_title: Pentbox Tutorial: Set Up a Honeypot in Kali Linux
74.seo_description: Set up a Pentbox honeypot in an isolated lab: install Ruby dependencies, navigate the menu, configure logging, test connections and review captured activity.

75.about: Chapter 75 returns to offense with browser exploitation. It distinguishes browser attacks from network exploits, lists vectors such as outdated plugins, malicious scripts and drive-by downloads, sets up BeEF in a lab, hooks a test browser, uses Metasploit against an outdated browser, delivers a payload, and explains why updates, script blockers and awareness defeat most of these attacks.
learn: What browser exploitation is and how it differs from network exploitation
Common browser attack vectors
How to set up BeEF and hook a test browser in a lab
What a hooked browser reveals to an attacker
How Metasploit browser exploit modules are used in a lab
Why updates, script blockers and user awareness are the main defences

concepts.p: Browser exploitation abuses the client rather than a network service. It often relies on outdated components or on convincing a user to visit a crafted page, which is why patching and script control matter more than network firewalls alone.

BeEF hooks a browser through injected JavaScript and exposes modules that show what page-level control can do. It is a demonstration framework: the value is understanding impact and defences, not attacking real users.

practical.intro: Use intentionally outdated browser instances in an isolated lab. BeEF is generally started as a service on Kali.

commands.d: Start the BeEF service.
Launch BeEF with the packaged configuration if the service is not used.
Open the BeEF control panel locally.
Start Metasploit for a lab browser exploit module.

practical.safety: Hooking a browser without consent is unauthorized access. Use only your own lab browsers and vintage VMs, and never host a hook on the public internet.

faq.q: What does it mean to hook a browser?
faq.a: A malicious or test page loads JavaScript that maintains a connection to the BeEF server, allowing the operator to run modules in that page context.

faq.q: How do I defend against browser exploitation?
faq.a: Keep the browser and plugins updated, remove unused extensions, use script blockers and enable automatic updates. User awareness reduces social-engineering success.

75.seo_title: Browser Exploitation with BeEF and Metasploit (Lab)
75.seo_description: Learn browser exploitation in a lab: BeEF setup and browser hooking, Metasploit browser modules, payload delivery, and the defences that stop this attack class.

76.about: The final chapter goes deeper into BeEF command modules. It recaps hooking a browser, tours the control panel and hooked-browser details, demonstrates social-engineering, information-gathering and persistence modules, chains a BeEF module with a Metasploit exploit, reviews session logs, and explains the defences: script blockers, CSP headers and updated browsers.
learn: How to navigate the BeEF control panel and browser details
How social-engineering modules manipulate what a user sees
What information modules reveal about a hooked browser
How persistence modules survive page navigation
How a BeEF module can be chained with a Metasploit exploit
How CSP, script blockers and updates defend against client-side attacks

concepts.p: BeEF modules run inside the hooked page's origin and browser context. They can manipulate the DOM, request resources and gather browser details, but the same-origin policy still constrains access to other sites.

A hook can gather information that helps choose a browser exploit, and a successful exploit can yield a deeper session. This is why client-side defence combines patching, content security policy and user awareness rather than relying on one control.

practical.intro: Continue in the isolated lab from the previous chapter. The video demonstrates module selection and the resulting panel output.

commands.d: Confirm the BeEF service is running.
Open the control panel and select the hooked browser.

practical.safety: Only hook browsers you own and control. Social-engineering modules can deceive users, and using them on real people without consent is unethical and often illegal.

faq.q: Does BeEF work if JavaScript is disabled?
faq.a: No. The hook depends on JavaScript execution in the page. Script blockers and strict policies prevent it.

faq.q: What is the best defence against BeEF-style attacks?
faq.a: Keep browsers updated, block untrusted scripts, deploy a restrictive Content Security Policy and educate users about suspicious pages.

76.seo_title: BeEF Hooked Browser Modules Explained (Kali Linux)
76.seo_description: Explore BeEF command modules: social engineering, browser information gathering, persistence, chaining with Metasploit, and defences like CSP and script blockers.
